Fog, noontide calm, flotsam, and a lost ship fill out the volume. An old buccaneer's song completes a sailor-poet's log in verse.
43897-antoine-of-oregon-a-story-of-the-o:
James Otis wrote a story of the Oregon Trail for boys, copyrighted in 1912 under his real name of Kaler. A map illustrates the story. Its narrator, Antoine, tells why he is not a fur trader, and how an unexpected proposition set him out as a guide.

The contents are a gazetteer of the trail: St Louis, the camp at Independence, the start under John Mitchell's outfit, and hardships to come. Wild horses overrun the camp, Pawnees are faced and taught a lesson, and Colonel Kearny's dragoons appear twice. Buffalo country, Fort Laramie, Fort Bridger, and Fort Hall follow, with hunting, stampedes, and scarce fuel between. A boy guide's education is the thread.
44037-the-adventures-of-billy-topsail:
Norman Duncan's The Adventures of Billy Topsail was published by Fleming Revell in 1906, with the author's other books priced at the front. The Mother stands at a dollar twenty-five, Doctor Luke of the Labrador at a dollar fifty, and Dr Grenfell's Parish at a dollar net. Duncan thanks the editors of the Youth's Companion for leave to reprint much of the book. The frontispiece shows a boy whose clothes froze stiff, beaten on the ice to soften them.

The adventures belong to the Labrador coast world of Duncan's other tales. Billy's story is told as a boy's book, but the cold in that frontispiece is the real thing: a Newfoundland lad's life among ice, boats, and fishing stations. The dedication leaf carries a short address to the boy who reads, and the tale then takes Billy out into that northern world.
44325-the-great-american-fraud-the-paten:
The Great American Fraud, by Samuel Hopkins Adams, gathers his Collier's Weekly articles on the patent medicine evil, the first printed on October 7, 1905. Adams warns that the series will expose the methods of the trade and the harm it does the public. He counts the cost at some seventy-five millions of dollars a year, paid by a gullible America.

For that money, he says, buyers swallow alcohol, opiates, and heart depressants, and above all, undiluted fraud. The six articles move from Peruna and the bracers to Liquozone, the subtle poisons, cures promised to the incurable, and the fundamental fakes. A second part charges the trade with a plot against the freedom of the press. The series helped push governments toward action, and it stands as a high mark of the muckraking years.
44600-martha-of-california-a-story-of-th:
Martha of California is a story of the California Trail by James Otis, in his pioneer series. The American Book Company issued the series for school and home reading. Companion tales follow Antoine of Oregon, Benjamin of Ohio, and Hannah of Kentucky. Seth of Colorado and Philip of Texas complete the six pioneer child stories.

A map illustrates Martha journey west in the front of the school edition. The copyright of 1913 stands in the name of the author wife, Mrs Kaler. Wagons, rivers, plains, and the Sierra crossing fill a girl view of the trail. Otis wrote hundreds of such brisk, honest books for American boys and girls.
44939-children-of-the-soil:
Children of the Soil is a novel by Henryk Sienkiewicz in English dress. Jeremiah Curtin made the approved full translation from the Polish text. Little Brown of Boston issued this edition in nineteen seventeen. The Polish rights date to eighteen ninety five in Curtin name.

A list of Sienkiewicz works fronts the book, from With Fire and Sword on. The Deluge, Pan Michael, Quo Vadis, and Without Dogma stand among them. Curtin Englished most of those famed Polish historical novels as well. Readers of this volume get Sienkiewicz in his tale of Polish land life. The book sits in the run of his works that won world fame.
44987-the-pioneer-trail:
Alfred Lambourne wrote The Pioneer Trail, published by the Deseret News at Salt Lake City in 1913 and dedicated to the memory of his father. The book replaces his earlier, out-of-print An Old Sketch-Book and The Old Journey. Lambourne says the new volume answers a demand for the original works, with much added matter.

He warns buyers that the character of the work has changed. It is now more an epitome of human emotion than a description of scenery. The narrative opens beside a steep mountain road, edged with wild-cherry, evergreens, and ancient shrub-oak. Wagon ruts have washed into deep gullies, and only shepherds now pass that way. Lambourne, an artist of Utah, writes the Mormon pioneer road as memory and feeling, not mere topography.
45065-english-pictures-drawn-with-pen-an:
English Pictures Drawn with Pen and Pencil is an illustrated description of English scenery by Samuel Manning and Green, published in 1889. The preface opens with a story. A British nobleman travelling in Switzerland was so struck by the gloomy grandeur of a mountain pass that he cried there was no other view like it in the world. His guide answered that there was one, in the Scottish Highlands.

Why, replied the nobleman, that is on my own estate, and I have never seen it. The editors grant the tale may be doubtful in fact but true in idea. The number of Englishmen who really know their own country, they say, is comparatively few. Hard-worked men flee abroad at intervals and return more jaded than they left. Yet within less than a day's journey, the tired city dweller may find quiet retreats.
45485-the-sky-trail:
Graham Dean, author of Daring Wings and Circle Four Patrol, wrote this aviation novel for boys. The Goldsmith Publishing Company of Chicago copyrighted it in 1932. Its hero is Tim Murphy, flying reporter and aviation editor of the Atkinson News, restless on a grey winter noon as the edition roars off the press.

Tim pecks at a story about a car accident and longs to soar in the Good News, the paper's biplane, grounded for an overhaul and a new motor. His flying companion Ralph Graves has been chasing fire trucks through mud and slush. Then the airport manager telephones that the plane is ready for a test flight, and the two cut lunch to take the hop. At that moment a deep rumble shakes the building, windows rattle, smoke mounts, and the telephones cry out with news of a major disaster, the managing editor leaning close at Tim's desk.
45507-the-pony-rider-boys-in-louisiana-o:
Frank Gee Patchin takes the Pony Rider Boys to Louisiana in this 1924 Altemus volume, following the game trails in the canebrake. The contents give each chapter in telegraph style. Southern hospitality opens the trip, with the fat boy, Stacy Brown, called Chunky. The boys pick out new ponies, show daring horsemanship for their girl friends, and head bound for the cane jungle.

Camp on Tensas Bayou means living with the snakes, while barred owls make the night hideous. An explosion sets the tents ablaze, and the boys are marooned in a swamp for three days. Chunky swims with the alligators, and Tad Butler blazes a trail that amazes Bill Lilly, the guide. A swim in Tensas Lake, a fat boy hung up in a tree, and the quest of the phantom deer fill the middle chapters.
45582-jack-ranger-s-gun-club-or-from-sch:
Clarence Young's 1910 schoolboy adventure opens with a boat race, Jack Ranger declaring himself as ready as he ever shall be while Dock Snaith fusses over oarlocks. Chapters move from Washington Hall to the open trail.

Titles promise a bully, a snowstorm, a midnight feast, an alarm of fire, and the forming of the gun club. The trip west brings a broken train, thirst on the desert, the Bad Lands, deadly gas, captives, and a bear. Young also wrote the Motor Boys series and Jack Ranger's Schooldays. Cupples and Leon published the book at New York. The Jack Ranger books form a series of school and outdoor tales.
4605-basil:
Wilkie Collins dedicated Basil to his old friend Charles James Ward, and he says the main event of the story rests on a fact within his own knowledge. Where he shaped that fact into narrative, he tried to keep it touching on something real and true, whether from his own experience or from stories told to him. The novel runs in three parts, and it belongs to the early Victorian sensation school Collins helped to create.

Basil, a young gentleman, marries in secret below his rank, and the marriage drags him into family rage, shame, and revenge. Collins builds suspense through letters, confessions, and confrontations, while keeping a close eye on class and respectability. Readers get a gripping early sensation novel, darker and more personal than a simple mystery, about a rash promise and the long price it exacts.
46185-the-devil:
The Devil, by Ferenc Molnar, was produced in New York in 1908. Kennerley published the play that year. Herford adapted it by arrangement with the author. Savage first staged it at Hartford in July 1908. Milton directed, with help from Vienna's Volks-Theatre chief. A cast list opens the printed play. Karl Mahler is an artist; Heinrich, his valet. Olga Hofmann, a banker's wife, stands fourth. The Devil himself calls himself Dr Miller. Elsa Berg, an heiress, completes the chief names. Three acts divide the action. The first is set in Karl's studio in Vienna, of an afternoon.

The second moves to the Hofmanns' reception room that evening. The third returns to the studio next morning. Long stage directions build the artist's rooms in detail.
46512-how-to-succeed-as-an-inventor-show:
Goodwin Smith, a registered patent lawyer at the United States Patent Office, wrote How to Succeed as an Inventor, issued in Philadelphia in 1909. The full title brags of great wealth to be made in new ideas, and warns of the risks on the way. Smith also held posts in firms built on patents of his own time.

Seventeen parts look back at past wins, name the fields most in need of new tools, and list the steps from first sketch to market. He teaches how to test demand, cut cost, file for a patent, and sell the rights. A tale at the front notes raw iron at twenty dollars a ton can earn far more as watch springs.
46694-under-sail:
Lincoln Colcord wrote sea tales drawn from a life before the mast. Eveleigh Nash and Grayson issued Under Sail in London in 1922. Six tales fill the set, from An Instrument of the Gods to Anjer. The title tale stands fourth among the gathered stories.

Sailors yarn under the after awning of the old Omega off Hong Kong. Nichols argues that East and West differ less than men like to claim. We fail to grasp even our best friends, he says in the harbor dark. Sea readers gain wise, salt tales from the last days of sail.
4684-the-u-p-trail:
Zane Grey's The U. P. Trail takes the building of the Union Pacific railroad as its epic subject. Grey opens by marvelling at how the line was pushed through unwatered wilderness and haunts of savage tribes. At each stage of construction, roaring, impromptu cities full of gold, lust, and death sprang up, then died away, leaving only wayside stations in the desert.

Chinese workers laboured beside border ruffians and broken men from Europe, gambling, drinking, quarrelling, and murdering like wolves. Yet the whole turmoil was directed by gentlemen in frock-coats, seeking a fortune and a later visit to Paris. Grey treats the railroad as the typical achievement of its age, joining all ranks and all ends of the world in one plot. Readers get a big western novel of iron, gold, and human ambition.
46866-the-adventures-of-peter-cottontail:
Thornton W Burgess tells how Peter Rabbit frets over his plain name in a Little, Brown tale from Boston dated 1917. Harrison Cady drew the plates, and Burgess names past books such as The Adventures of Reddy Fox at the front. Peter sits in the Old Briar-patch with a scowl on a bright spring day.

Peter gripes that no one would mark a great deed done by a plain Peter Rabbit. Jimmy Skunk pokes his head into a private path and grins at the talk he has heard. Jimmy then rhymes the moral: a name holds just what we put in it by deed and word. Merry Little Breezes dance and birds sing while Peter hangs his head in shame at his folly.
47246-a-deal-with-the-devil:
Eden Phillpotts wrote A Deal with the Devil, published at London in 1895. Twenty-four chapters open with Grandfather's Birthday and close with The Passing of Grandpapa. Before Mr Daniel Dolphin comes down to breakfast on his hundredth birthday, his granddaughter Martha tells us about him.

He has been married three times and buried all his wives and all his children, five of them. Martha, only child of his eldest, is what remains. Chapters run In the Cupboard, Cold Comfort, Hidden in London, and Vote for Dolphin. Marie Rogers, the squire's daughter, a crusade, and counsel's opinion fill the middle. I forbid the banns brings the climax. Readers get a Devon novelist's tale of a centenarian and his bargain.
48228-averil:
Rosa Nouchette Carey's novel appeared as number 8 of the Arm Chair Library, a weekly issue sold for ten cents, from Lupton in New York in February 1896. Each number of the library contained a complete novel by a popular author. The story opens on a wet day in Lincoln's Inn, in Harland's chambers.

Harland is a thorough optimist, a man of easy temper whom no fog, east wind, or run of wet days can depress. May has come in with a February chill, the rain pours, and he warms his hands at the fire his housekeeper has lit, glad of a quiet morning without fussy clients. His wife, who matches him in good humor, is said by her friends to be a fortunate woman.
48414-an-account-of-the-bell-rock-light-:
Robert Stevenson, engineer to the Northern Lighthouse Board, tells how a lighthouse rose on a drowned reef in a report issued at Edinburgh in 1824. Archibald Constable published it. Twenty-three engravings fill the book, one drawn by J M W Turner.

Bell Rock lies about eleven miles off the Scottish shore. It long stood as an object of dread to mariners bound for the Firths of Forth and Tay. Stevenson wrote the account at the wish of the Commissioners of the Northern Light-Houses. A history of that body and its progress fronts the tale. The main text gives the erection and peculiar structure of the edifice in full detail. Stevenson founded a dynasty of lighthouse engineers. This book is the founding record.
48680-the-border-boys-on-the-trail:
The Border Boys on the Trail is a boys' adventure novel by Fremont Deering. Hurst issued it in New York in 1911. The contents list runs to twenty-four chapters. Two boys of about seventeen ride a train to the border. The first chapter lands them in a small New Mexico town. Trainmen shout its name, Maguez, as the express rolls in.

The chapters promise rustlers, escapes, and a treasure. A race for life comes early in the list. The boys fall into enemy hands, then ride for the hills. A hermit of the canyon and a prospector enter the tale. The treasure of the mission waits near the close. Rurales and a round-up end the action. Border tales fed on the Mexican frontier setting. Deering's series gave boys that ground in book after book.
48947-boy-scouts-on-the-trail:
John Garth wrote this Boy Scouts adventure, copyrighted in 1920 and published with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Chapter one opens at the camp on Long Point, where Harry Ritter is reading the camp paper in the shade. He calls out gleefully over a story that Bull Taggart has been chased by a shark in the Sound.

The contents promise a full camp programme of trouble. A man in a dory, Loon Island, a lightning flash, and a plot lead toward a night ride through storm and darkness. Later chapters bring a haunted cabin, a hidden wireless, a disappearance, a rescue and escape, and a lonely soldier, before the parting of the ways.
48960-travels-in-brazil:
Travels in Brazil is a travel account by Henry Koster, printed in London by Longman in 1816. Koster inscribes the travels to Robert Southey, the poet laureate, in memorial of affectionate respect and gratitude. His preface is a modest one. During his residence in Brazil, he says, he had no intention of publishing any account of what he had seen and heard.

Some time after his return to England, friends encouraged him to put together what information he could impart. The idiom of a foreign language is perhaps more familiar to him than his own. The contents begin with a visit to the governor, the climate, and a first ride into the country. A village near Recife, Olinda, and the Holy Week feasts of Thursday, Friday, and Easter follow. Koster's book became a classic of Brazilian travel.
50105-grace-harlowe-s-overland-riders-on:
Grace Harlowe Overland Riders on the Old Apache Trail, by Jessie Graham Flower, was held under a 1921 copyright and printed at Philadelphia. Flower wrote the long Grace Harlowe line, from high school and college tales to war tales with the Red Cross and the troops.

The Overton girls plan a summer outing in the saddle, and Hippy holds a dark secret. Emma Dean says no weak lemonade trips for her. The girls vote for a night ride on the old Deadwood stage coach, in spite of loud protests from those inside. Later notes tell of a coach lost off a cliff and a hard walk on foot. Readers get trail peril, pluck, and girl team work in the West.
50464-the-lonesome-trail:
John Neihardt wrote these western tales, published by Lane in New York and London in 1907. A race with the fire, drawn by Schoonover, fronts the book from one story. Lines from Henley's 'Invictus' stand as the young poet's motto on the title page.

Neihardt was a Nebraska poet who had ridden and traded in the Missouri country he writes of. Cowboys, Indians, fire and flood fill the tales of his lonesome trail here. The Nemesis of the Deuces, named in the plate's caption, is among them, in an early book from the man who later wrote 'Black Elk Speaks' in fame.
5067-the-rainbow-trail:
Zane Grey's Rainbow Trail returns to the desert country of Riders of the Purple Sage, answering a question readers often asked about that romance's ending. Grey opens with the desert's spell returning: veils like purple smoke in the canyon, silence, and the strange wild life of the last American wilderness, wild still almost as it ever was.

The story follows the trail to the foot of the rainbow, through the Grand Canyon of the Colorado to Willow Springs, in chapters that mix romance, pursuit, and canyon scenery. Grey notes the tale first appeared serially in a different form. Readers get a western sequel that stands alone, lush with desert color and frontier feeling.
51452-those-holy-fields-palestine-illust:
Those Holy Fields, Palestine illustrated by pen and pencil, is a travel book by Samuel Manning. The Religious Tract Society published it in London from Paternoster Row. Manning is named as author of Italian Pictures, Swiss Pictures, and Spanish Pictures on the title page. A drawing of the range of Hermon near Banias, the main source of the Jordan, fronts the book.

Banias, or Caesarea Philippi, is named on that plate as the probable scene of the Transfiguration. The book tours the Holy Land for readers who knew its places from the Bible at home. Manning pen and the artists pencils together made Palestine visible to Victorian parlours. Such illustrated tours were the armchair pilgrimage of the age, sold by a society whose aim was devotion as much as geography for its buyers.
51688-the-air-of-castor-oil:
The Air of Castor Oil is a science fiction tale by Jim Harmon, printed in Galaxy Magazine in August 1961. Pictures by Walker go with it. The tale is told in the first person by a man who keeps telling himself that now, at last, it is safe to do the thing he aches to do.

He walks past a radio store where a colour television set plays a quiz show to no one. In his pocket sits a newspaper account of a great rocket that failed and burned out. Down the back streets, past brick walls and small foreign cars, he makes for a little shop he left long ago: the Back Number Store.
5194-the-ivory-trail:
Talbot Mundy's Ivory Trail opens with a song of Zanzibar, greener than emeralds and whiter than diamonds. It follows ivory hunters and adventurers into East Africa. Chapters move through slave gangs, a great game reserve, and songs of elephants and dark lords, as the trail leads inland toward fortune and danger.

Mundy writes of the ivory trade, its hunters, traders, and porters, with the pace of popular adventure. The novel offers a vivid, if dated, picture of early twentieth-century Africa as imagined by a writer who knew the region's stories well. It remains one of his best known African tales.
5233-the-iron-trail:
Rex Beach's Iron Trail is set in Alaska. A tide, a girl appearing out of the night, and an Irish prince open a story of railroads and rivalry. Chapters follow a journey to Hope, the dreamer and his dream, the villain Curtis Gordon. The novel explores Eliza Violet Appleton's two sides, toward a battle at Gordon's crossing.

Beach mixes frontier adventure with business intrigue, as men fight over a railway route through wild country. The novel offers readers the Alaska of the gold-rush era, with storms, camps. Strong personalities carry the story, told at the brisk pace of popular adventure fiction.
52358-the-desert-trail:
The Desert Trail is a Western novel by Dane Coolidge, author of Bat Wing Bowles, published in 1915. Douglas Duer and PJ Monahan drew the pictures.

The first chapter opens at dawn in Gadsden, a border city where the main street runs south from the railroad and stops dead at the line of Mexico. A hundred miles of desert, dry arroyos, and sandy plains lie beyond. In the warming morning the town fills with men driven in from below the line: Texas cattlemen, mining men with deserted mines, millmen, and ranchers. A hundred petty chiefs below the border stand out against Madero and live by ransom and loot. The Americans must cool their heels in Gadsden and wait for the end to come, and the tale starts among them.
52385-dick-kent-with-the-malemute-mail:
Milton Richards wrote a boys' tale of the far north, printed at Akron, Ohio in 1927. Dick Kent rides again, in a line of books with the mounted police, the Eskimos, and the fur trade. Contents promise a creeping threat and an inspector who takes charge.

Smoke, a fire patrol, and a Mackenzie River post come early. Later heads name ships from the stars, a toll of the north, a mutineer, and shapes in the storm. A lone cabin, a chase, and a night patrol lead to the trek home. The tale opens on a worn, ragged man crossing a bleak, sun baked valley with no trail, in a wild land of sand and silt.
52949-under-sail:
Felix Riesenberg sails as a young hand on the square-rigged ship A J Fuller from New York to Honolulu and back. Macmillan issued his sea tale in September 1918, with plates of crew men and ports. He gives the book to Maud, and a long contents list maps the full voyage leg by leg.

Chapters cover Christmas Day on the high seas, a fight, and Neptune coming on board in the old sea rite. Life in the fo'c'sle, Cape Horn twice, and a man lost overboard mark the hard parts of the run. In port, the crew unloads, loads sugar, and tastes town life in old Honolulu. An opening essay hails the square riggers as America turns back to the sea in war time.
54141-a-party-in-mother-goose-land-a-one:
A Party in Mother Goose Land is a one-act play for small school children by Effa Preston. It was published by the Paine Publishing Company of Dayton, Ohio, with copyright in 1922. The front matter sells song sheets for school shows at thirty-five cents each.

The play brings nursery figures to a party. Mother Goose wears an old dress and a tall pointed hat. Boy Blue carries a horn and calls out the guests. Hansel and Gretel come as a pair. Robinson Crusoe wears rags. Jack the Giant Killer bears a large sword, and Puss in Boots wears a cat mask and high boots. Goldilocks comes with yellow hair. The costume notes leave much to the teacher, who may make the dress plain or grand as she likes.
54630-camp-lenape-on-the-long-trail:
Camp Lenape on the Long Trail is a boys' camp novel by Carl Saxon, printed at New York. Saxon also wrote Blackie Thorne at Camp Lenape and The Mystery at Camp Lenape. Copyright entries of 1935 and 1940 stand on its page. Eighteen chapters run from A Feud Begins to The End of the Trail.

The tale opens behind the Lenape lodge, where Brick Ryan wrings out his only flannel shirt. A shiny limousine roars up the road into camp, and Brick whistles at the golden chariot. Out steps a worried lady covered in diamonds, come about her son Dirk. Ahead lie the sinking of the Sachem, a forest fire, and the Long Trail itself.
55282-work-travail:
Émile Zola wrote Work, translated by Ernest Alfred Vizetelly and published at London in 1901. Book one opens as Luc Froment walks out of Beauclair at random. He climbs the Brias road, following the gorge where the Mionne torrent flows between the Bleuse mountains.

Before the Abyss, as the Qurignon steel-works are called locally, he sees two dark, puny creatures shrinking against the parapet of the wooden bridge. One is a very young woman, poorly clad, her head half hidden in ragged wool. The other, nestling in her skirts, is a white-faced child of about six, scarcely clothed at all. Both fix their eyes on the works door, waiting with the patience of despair. Readers get the second of Zola's Four Gospels, labour's suffering and its promised city.
56171-a-journey-in-brazil:
A Journey in Brazil is a book of trips and of wild lore by the Agassiz pair, the teach man and his wife. It was put out at Boston in eighteen sixty eight. The host print is the next form of the book. A verse from a bard of the land stands past the title leaf. The book is sworn to the friend who made it in his might to give this trip the cast of a lore trip.

The first words tell how the trip came to be. In the cold time of eighteen sixty five the teach man had to seek a change of scene for his health. He need rest from work as well. The old world was put forth as the place for that rest.
56220-historical-record-of-the-seventh-r:
The Historical Record of the Seventh Regiment, or the Royal Fusiliers, belongs to Richard Cannon's series of Historical Records of the British Army. The series was made by command of King William the Fourth, under the patronage of the Queen, and printed by authority at the Adjutant General's Office, Horse Guards.

General orders dated January 1, 1836, set the pattern every volume follows. Each record must give the regiment's first raising, its stations, and the battles and sieges where it fought. The names of officers and men killed or wounded, and of those marked out for gallant conduct, must all be set down. Badges and devices borne by the regiment, and the causes for them, close the account.
56602-frank-hunter-s-peril:
Frank Hunter's Peril, by Horatio Alger Junior, was printed at Philadelphia by Henry T Coates, with a copyright of 1896. The front plate shows Katy O'Grady's victory, and the tale opens on a lawn. Mr Craven calls too often on Frank's widowed mother, and Frank, cold at the gate, does not like the man. His friend Ben Cameron names the fear in jest: a step-father in the making. Craven's courtship runs through the first heads.

Then the plot thickens: a plot against Frank, a trap, and a trip to London and the Paris fair. A hotel by a glacier, a brink, and a search fill the last acts. Colonel Sharpley's ruse turns at last to just deserts. Boys of the age got Alger grit: a lad's rights held fast against wealth and guile.
5718-the-great-salt-lake-trail:
Colonel Henry Inman traces the history of the trail to the Great Salt Lake through explorers, trappers, traders, and soldiers. Chapters cover expeditions from 1774 onward. They treat the old trappers and their outfits, trading posts, and the Mormons. They also treat the Pony Express, the stage route to the Pacific, and the Union Pacific Railroad. Later chapters turn to Sioux traditions, the Crows, Blackfeet lore, Buffalo Bill, and Custer's command.

The book works as a fireside history, gathering camp stories, local color, and frontier incident into one long narrative. Readers meet Jim Beckwourth, Kit Carson, and many lesser-known guides, and they see how a trail became a road, then a railroad. It suits readers of western history who enjoy anecdote-rich storytelling alongside the larger sweep of settlement.
57988-a-son-of-the-soil:
Oliphant wrote a novel in a new form dated 1872, set on a Scots farm named Ramore. Rain beats down as a glib young guest mocks the wet land and its folk from the porch. Young Colin burns to snap back, held in check by the sound of his mothers voice in the house.

The farmer, Colin of Ramore, meets scorn with calm wit and a bid to dry boots by his fire. His lads, he says with a proud twinkle, take small heed of rain or shine at their work. Town gloss and soil grit clash at first sight, and pride on both sides sets the tale in train.
59402-betting-gambling-a-national-evil:
B Seebohm Rowntree edited a set of essays on betting and gambling as a national evil, published in London in 1905. The York Anti Gambling League committee prompted the work, and Rowntree dedicated it to them. John A Hobson opens with the ethics of gambling. He defines gambling as settling who owns property by appeal to chance.

John Hawke treats the extent of gambling and the existing law. Other essays cover stock exchange gambling, gambling among women, and crime and gambling. A bookmaker writes on the deluded sportsman. J Ramsay MacDonald writes on gambling and citizenship. Appendices give Lords' recommendations, a street betting bill, statistics, and a bibliography.
59887-virgil:
Lucas Collins wrote this study of Virgil for a classics series. Blackwood printed the book at Edinburgh and London in 1870. Conington death left the volume to Collins, the preface owns. Contents move from the poet life to Pastorals and Georgics first.

The Aeneid takes the bulk, told book by book in chapters. Shipwreck at Carthage, the fall of Troy, and Dido open it. Funeral games, the Sibyl and shades, and Latium landing follow. Death of Pallas, Camilla, and the last combat close the survey. Virgil poems served as school text books within fifty years of his death, Collins notes.
60118-casa-grande-ruins-trail:
Park Service staff wrote this trail booklet for Casa Grande Ruins in Arizona. The monument is one of more than 280 Park Service areas. A map of Compound A and a safety note open the guide. Desert heat, cactus spines, and rare venomous animals earn a warning.

The trail runs about four hundred yards, an easy walk for most. Numbered stakes match numbered notes in the booklet at each stop. Visitors may enter the Big House only with a ranger guide. Law bars hunting, woodcutting, and taking even shards of pottery there.
60968-the-sexual-life-of-our-time-in-its:
Iwan Bloch, a Berlin physician for diseases of the skin and the sexual system, wrote The Sexual Life of Our Time. Eden Paul translated it from the sixth German edition; Rebman printed it at London in 1909. Sale of the English version was limited to the legal and medical professions.

The publishers call the book a complete encyclopedia of the sexual sciences. Chapters treat the basic facts of human love, the brain and senses, and the marks that divide the sexes in body and mind. Later chapters take up religion and sexuality, shame, dress, and nakedness. Cases from practice fill the pages.
61089-roy-blakeley-s-tangled-trail:
Roy Blakeley's Tangled Trail is a Boy Scout novel by Percy Keese Fitzhugh, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1924. It was issued with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America and illustrated by Barbour. Fitzhugh wrote the Tom Slade books, the Pee-Wee Harris books, and the rest of the Blakeley shelf.

The contents open with greetings and a chapter on the shelf. Hervey and the camp, tracks, and plans lead to the start. The fall of Scout Harris, foiled again, and the sound of merry laughter carry the fun. Girls and wasps, a character called the Shiveller, and hands off follow. Jelly cones, ancient history, and a story of the past fill the middle. A rare species and thirty-four cents stand among the later chapters. Roy narrates in his own breathless voice, tangling the trail as only a scout camp can.
61596-the-aeneid-of-virgil:
Rolfe Humphries turned Virgil's Aeneid into English verse in this translation, published in New York by Scribner with a preface dated January 1951. Humphries gave the book to the memory of his father, his first and best Latin teacher. The poem opens with the famous line: arms and the man I sing, the exile driven by fate from Troy to the coast of Italy.

The twelve books follow the old order: the landing near Carthage, the fall of Troy, the wanderings of Aeneas, and his love and parting from Dido. Funeral games, the descent to the lower world, and war in Italy fill the later books. The last book ends in the final combat. Humphries keeps a clear, swift line that lets English readers follow the whole arc of Rome's founding epic without notes at every step.
61894-the-world-struggle-for-oil:
Pierre l'Espagnol de la Tramerye's The World-Struggle for Oil, turned from the French by Leese, was published by Alfred Knopf of New York in February 1924. The contents open with a blunt motto for the whole: who has oil has empire. Four parts sort the fight by trusts, by powers, and by France's share in it.

The trusts come first: the Standard Oil Company, the Royal Dutch-Shell, and Henry Deterding, named oil's Napoleon. Then the powers: a German trust wrecked by the war, Britain and the United States at odds in Mexico, and the state-backed Anglo-Persian company. A late run of chapters tells how the United States lost the lead in oil, and what answer it made, from Washington to Genoa.
62335-the-unpublished-legends-of-virgil:
Charles Godfrey Leland dug up fresh folk tales of Virgil as a mage. His book came out in London in 1899. He gave it to Comparetti, who wrote on Virgil in the Middle Ages. Leland wrote from Florence in September of that year. Old tales made Virgil a great mage in the dark ages, he notes.

Dante made Virgil known to all folk, Leland holds. So more tales of him must still live in mouth lore, he thought. He and his aids gleaned about one score tales times five. Just three or four share a plot with the old set. Tale fans get a new hoard of odd lore.
62946-grace-harlowe-s-overland-riders-on:
Grace Harlowe Overland Riders on the Lost River Trail is by Jessie Flower, published at Philadelphia, copyright 1924. Flower had written the High School Girls and College Girls series.

Contents are given with lively chapter notes. Chapter one is a mystery of the night. There is peril in the air, the guide warns, and the Overlanders take flight. The party is threatened by a forest fire, and hastens to help imperilled villagers. Chapter two is in the demon grip. Inhabitants of Silver Creek mock a warning, then are aroused at last. The fire demon roars, and Miss Briggs narrowly escapes. Readers get a girls trail adventure with fire, flight, and rescue.
62947-the-balkan-trail:
The Balkan Trail, by Frederick Moore, records travel in the Balkans with 62 illustrations and a map, published by Smith, Elder and Company at London in 1906. Chapters run from the Bulgarian border and the road to Rilo through Sofia and the Bulgarians, Constantinople and the Turks, and Salonica and the Jews.

Moore goes on to the dynamiters, Monastir and the Greeks, Uskub and the Serbs, and Metrovitza and the Albanians, ending on the trail of the insurgent and the track of the Turk. Gilbert Holiday drew the frontispiece. The route took Moore across country on horseback and on foot.
63334-ireland-in-travail:
Joice Nankivell and Sydney Loch wrote this account of Ireland in travail, printed in London in 1922. The two authors take turns at the chapters, signing them with their initials, as they settle in Dublin and watch the fight for Ireland up close. The contents read like a diary of the troubled years: crossing to Dublin after curfew, finding a flat, and making acquaintances.

A chapter traces the birth of Sinn Fein from the Celtic revival. Later chapters cover the hunger strike, Bloody Sunday, and the height of the terror, with reprisals, raids, and wanted men. The writers meet a minister of propaganda, see a cabinet minister captured, and end inside Dublin Castle itself. The book treats Ireland as a land in pain while a new state struggles to be born.
63552-armazindy-the-poems-and-prose-sket:
James Whitcomb Riley's poems and prose sketches were gathered in a Homestead Edition volume printed at New York in 1917. Armazindy leads the book, named for a Hoosier girl whose family name was Ballenger, as her daddy answered it in the old war records. The volume is given to Henry Eitel. The old trundle bed and natural perversities follow the title poem.

The old school chum, writing back to the home folks, the blind girl, and we defer things fill the early pages. The Muskingum valley, for this Christmas, a poor man's wealth, and the little red ribbon come next. How did you rest last night, a good bye, and when Maimie married stand in the roll. Riley writes Indiana farms in warm dialect, and Armazindy herself won the good will of all the neighborhood, as the poem says.
63847-garden-of-evil:
Garden of Evil is a science fiction tale by Margaret St Clair, printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1949. Its hero Ericson is a student of peoples who has sunk into drug use, and the planet Fyhon is to him a paradise. The prize of the tale is Dridihad, a secret city of dread, worth any man's life to find.

Ericson wakes from a long fog of pain with a green skinned girl, Mnathl, feeding him roasted meat by a lake. Months of his life are a blank edged with hurt. He recalls begging food in the streets of Penhairn before she led him toward Lake Tanais, and the pain that began from there.
63925-a-blockaded-family-life-in-souther:
Parthenia Antoinette Hague recalls wartime domestic life in A Blockaded Family, published at Boston and New York in 1888. Hague taught school on a plantation near Eufaula, Alabama, and stayed through the war years. Her chapters describe how a blockaded household met the emergency: dyeing cloth, making shoes, thread, hats and bonnets, and spinning homespun dresses with home-made buttons.

Other chapters give substitutes for coffee, raspberry-leaf tea, home-made starch, putty and cement, and the spinning bees around the fireside. The memoir opens in the summer of 1861 with a letter from her father: her brothers were leaving for Richmond as soldiers of the new Confederacy.
63944-tiger-by-the-tail:
Poul Anderson wrote Tiger by the Tail, a tale printed in Planet Stories in January 1951. Its hero is Captain Dominic Flandry, Terra's ace saboteur. The teaser sets his task: the haughty, horned aliens of Scotha mean to conquer the Terran Empire.

Flandry wakes with a hangover under a metal ceiling, aboard a ship on ultra-drive. He had gone to sleep in the stews of Catawrayannis, with no thought of leaving the city. The sheets are vegetable fibre, the blankets long bluish-gray hair, and the chairs hand-carved wood in a pattern new to him. Drugged, he decides, and carried off by someone from outside the Empire.
64230-the-venus-evil:
Chester S Geier wrote a tale of Venus first printed in Planet Stories in summer 1947. Richard Farris tells the tale as a forced account for the police. He states at once that he had to kill George Pearce on Venus. Pearce was a great chemist and one of three men on the first trip there.

Farris looks back to a first Mars rocket that came home rich with gold and gems. Greed then drove fast, flawed rockets that blew up or vanished. A rich genius named Anson Durwent built the Solarian for true research. What the crew found on Venus drives Farris to his grim act.
64244-preview-of-peril:
Preview of Peril is a science fiction story by Alfred Coppel the younger. It first reached print in a magazine called Planet Stories in September nineteen fifty three, the hosted note says. Its headnote tells of four ships of a flotilla slipping like shadows through a Martian patrol cordon. Only the crazy luck of their mad, medal decked commodore would get them out again, it adds.

The second Martian war was three weeks old when the tale opens. Officers of the Terran destroyer Darkside stand assembled in control. Their flotilla commodore is sizing them up, the text says. Having a flag officer aboard is a hardship on a small ship, it notes. Five of nine officers must double up on cabin space. The easy life of an informal vessel will vanish too.
64456-the-strange-friend-of-tito-gil:
The Strange Friend of Tito Gil is a novel by Pedro de Alarcón, turned into English by Mrs Darr. The English text bears a copyright of 1890 and was issued in New York. Tito Gil is a poor boy of about nineteen, tall, thin, and bright in spirit.

Tito was the son of Juan Gil, a shoemaker to the old court, and his mother died at his birth. The Count of Rionuevo, a rich client of the shop, took pity on the boy and brought him to his palace as a page. There Tito learned Latin from a friar, in spite of the Countess and her sharp jabs at his low birth. The tale tracks his rise and the strange friend of its title.
64629-sticks-and-stones-a-study-of-ameri:
Lewis Mumford published Sticks and Stones, a study of American architecture and civilization, at New York in 1924. Mottos from Lethaby and Matthew Arnold frame the theme: architecture, properly understood, is civilization itself. Seven chapters carry the story from medieval roots to the machine age.

Contents run through the medieval tradition, the heritage of the Renaissance, and the classical myth. Later chapters treat the diaspora of the pioneer, the defeat of romanticism, and the imperial façade. A final chapter joins architecture and civilization outright. His first chapter recalls a community type that flourished in early America. Readers get Mumford's first book, reading American building as American history.
64682-the-painted-veil:
Somerset Maugham wrote The Painted Veil, here in the collected edition of his works from Heinemann. A line at the front gives the title sense: the painted veil which those who live call Life. The tale opens in a shuttered room, dark in the heat of the day. A woman and a man speak in whispers, and she cries out in fear. Some one has just tried the door of the room, she says.

It cannot be her husband Walter, she holds, since he stays at his laboratory till five. Nor would the servants come at the hour of sleep after tiffin. Her lover fumbles with tight shoes while she slips on a wrap and hands him a shoe-horn. Maugham sets a scene of guilt and dread in spare strokes.
64745-flowering-evil:
Flowering Evil is a science fiction story by Margaret St. Clair, printed in Planet Stories in the summer of 1950. Its heroine is Amy Dinsmore, a keen gardener whose nephew Robert sends her plants from far-off worlds. Her newest prize is a Venusian Rambler, which she hopes will win a prize at the flower show.

Captain Bjornson warns her that Robert's gifts have hurt her before. One cutting swelled her face for two weeks, and a cactus once filled her skin with spines. She will not hear a word against the boy or the plant. The Rambler's own hopes, hinted on the title page, give the tale its chill. It is a neat, dry pulp story about pride in a garden.
64982-the-tale-of-bunny-cotton-tail:
Laura Rountree Smith tells how a young rabbit burns his paw and flees into a garden in a Flanagan tale held under rights from 1904. A Flanagan Company of Chicago and New York issued the story for small children. A verse plate shows little Bunny who read by candle-light when small and now goes to bed at night.

Chapter one grants that the tale might never have been written had Bunny not read late by candle. He waves a paw too near the flame in his thrill over a story and burns it badly. Mother Cotton-Tail ties the paw in a cabbage leaf, which Bunny eats for its fine smell in bed. He then creeps out at night, against his mother's rule, and finds a garden of cabbages and a tall scare-crow.
65070-what-so-proudly-we-hail:
Day Keene wrote a time slip tale that ran in Imagination in December 1950. Ephraim Hale wakes after a night of hot buttered rum at the Pig and Whistle in 1789. He had served in the army and now sits for Middlesex in the first Congress at New York. He finds himself naked, robbed, and far from his own time.

The head note says Central Park in 1950 is a far cry from his inn. Hale must prove who he is with a letter from Sam Osgood about a post office post. Keene plays the clash of eras for humor and unease. A man of the early republic faces a modern city.
65126-an-eel-by-the-tail:
Eel by the Tail is a science fiction story by Allen K Lang. It first reached print in a magazine of science and fantasy in April nineteen fifty one, the hosted note says. Its headnote sets the puzzle: a strip tease dancer appeared in a physics classroom. Her being there made no sense to her teacher. How she got there bothered him more, the note adds.

Mr Tedder, the teacher, is fresh out of college in his first job. His class in second year physics is a tough one, full of hardened boys sure of themselves. He spent a month of after school hours studying a little known electrical effect. He hoped a show of that effect might shock the class awake. He wound his coils with more care for drama than for good sense, the tale says.
66015-history-of-the-forty-eighth-regime:
History of the Forty Eighth Regiment of Massachusetts volunteers during the Civil War tells the story of one nine months regiment. Albert Plummer served as its historian. Plates show its colonel, Eben Stone, and the generals over it, Banks and Augur of the Nineteenth Army Corps. Its chaplain, surgeon, and captains appear in turn.

One plate mourns Lieutenant Colonel James O'Brien, killed at Port Hudson in May 1863. Another shows the state house at Baton Rouge, burned in December 1862. In his preface Plummer calls his work a modest, true account of the regiment's service. He knows no such history can please everybody, and asks his comrades to judge it kindly. Regimental histories like this one kept the record of local men who marched south together. They list deeds, marches, and losses the big war histories pass by.
66209-to-sup-with-the-devil:
Myron Scholnick wrote this story, printed in Imagination in January 1954. Two friends, Henry and George, spend a friendly evening in soft leather chairs before a fireplace, talking pleasantly over their wine about a very unpleasant subject.

George is telling how he met the Devil last week and had an interesting chat with him. Henry, lips stained with wine, leans forward and urges him to continue, winking as if it were a joke. The firelight and the dark corners do the rest of the work. Readers get a fireside tale of the supernatural, told as after-dinner talk that may be more than talk.
66758-nick-carter-stories-no-139-may-8-1:
Nick Carter Stories number 139, dated 8 May 1915, carries the tale The Pressing Peril. Street and Smith issued the weekly at New York for dime novel readers. Ownership lines in the front name the Smith firm and its Seventh Avenue house. Such weeklies put a fresh Nick Carter case in the hands of readers each week.

Nick Carter was the most famed detective hero of the dime novel era. Each number threw him into a fresh peril, as this title promises in plain words. Short length, fast pace, and a cliff edge plot were the stock of the line. Boys and working readers formed the core buyers of such weeklies in 1915. The number survives as a sample of mass fiction in the United States before the pulps.
66844-the-life-of-the-weevil:
The Life of the Weevil, by J Henri Fabre, in English by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos, was printed in London by Hodder and Stoughton. The essays come from Fabre Souvenirs entomologiques, his famed insect memoirs. The translator gathered the weevil pieces into one volume.

In his note the translator says some chapters had stood in The Life and Love of the Insect and in Social Life in the Insect World. He was allowed to rework them for this full, final edition of Fabre works. Three or four volumes in the set treat beetles in all. Fabre writes of winter rest, when the insect sleeps and he turns to old coins for delight. He loves to question the metal disks, records of the small things men call history. Nature fans get close lives of snout beetles from a master watcher.
66966-legends-for-lionel-in-pen-and-penc:
Walter Crane draws and rhymes a picture book for a boy named Lionel. Cassell and Company issued it at London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne in 1887. Each page pairs a short verse with a drawing.

The tale starts in August, with Jack Frost sending his herald. Thaw and Fog follow, and Lionel looks out for Christmas. A stately Turkey opens a garden door. Attendant sausages and a plum pudding escort him in. Mince-pies, crackers, and a rain of bon-bons fill the feast. A snap-dragon breathes fire and St George follows. King Frost nips toes and noses in his freezing house. Green Spring sleeps in her car, tying up her posies. Crane led the Arts and Crafts book world. His toy books set the look of the nursery shelf.
6715-isobel-a-romance-of-the-northern-tr:
James Oliver Curwood sets Isobel on the northern trail, a thousand miles north of civilization at Point Fullerton. Sergeant William MacVeigh of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police writes his half-year report with a pencil stub. He hunts Scottie Deane, a murderer, for three hundred miles along Hudson's Bay. His search runs to Eskimo Point and north to Wagner Inlet. Hope has not left him yet.

Into that harsh hunt comes Isobel, and love grows where law and cold rule. Curwood writes with a northerner's love of snow, dogs, and lonely trails. Isobel is a stirring, romantic tale of the far north, where duty and heart pull a mounted policeman two ways.
67224-the-devil:
The Devil is a story by Leo Tolstoy, translated by Aylmer Maude. Allen and Unwin published it at London; it first appeared in 1926. Verses from Matthew stand at its head as a warning. Whoever looks on a woman in lust has already sinned in his heart, they say. Pluck out the eye and cut off the hand rather than fall. A list of Russian names, with stress accents marked, follows.

Eugene Irtenev, a landed proprietor, heads that list of persons. His wife Liza and his mother Mary stand near him. Stepanida, a peasant and another man's wife, enters the cast as well. Stewards, clerks, servants, and peasants fill out the estate world. Twenty one chapters and a variation carry the tale. Tolstoy's title names the power his hero cannot master. The names alone sketch a household built for temptation and ruin.
67418-the-wilderness-trail:
The Wilderness Trail is a frontier novel by Bedford-Jones, printed at London. Bedford-Jones also wrote Splendour of the Gods and The Kasbah Gate. The tale opens in the Kentucky wilderness in the year 1810. Backwoods folk counted it the thirty-fourth year of the Independence of the United States.

Settlers around Louisville were split over Federal or Democrat, and over Aaron Burr's great conspiracy. Tecumseh's allied hordes menaced them across the Indiana border. Law had come into the country, to many men's bitterness. Land titles had ousted men less famous than Daniel Boone himself. An old man, thewed like a giant, stands on the Beargrass Creek Road swearing at a horseman who spattered him with mud.
67627-the-treasure-trail:
Frank Pollock wrote The Treasure Trail, published at Boston in 1906 with a colour frontispiece by Louis Gowing. Twenty chapters run from The New Leaf to The Rainbow Road. The first chapter opens with Elliott murmuring over a letter while waiting with the horses for Margaret, who needed twelve minutes for her riding costume.

The letter comes from an old Colorado acquaintance now superintending a Transvaal gold mine. Chapters promise the fate of a treasure ship, the ace of diamonds, the mystery of the mate, and the indiscretion of Henninger. A lost clue, open war, first blood, and a battle on a lagoon follow. Readers get a treasure-hunt romance spanning oceans.
67823-the-lone-trail:
Luke Allan wrote this Canadian western, published by Jenkins in London in a British printing. The murder at the T-Inverted R opens the contents with a ranch brand for a name. Morton Stamford, a tenderfoot, enters in chapter two of the chapter list at the front.

Corporal Faircloth of the mounted police arrives third, and shots from the bushes follow. Dakota runs amok, a lamb walks among lions and fossil hunters appear in the middle chapters. The conspiracy, riders of the night, a secret valley and a fight in the ranch house carry Allan's tale of the Alberta foothills at a gallop.
68006-recoil:
George Smith wrote the story Recoil for Astounding Science-Fiction, where it appeared in November 1943. Orban drew the story's pictures. Walter Franks is acting director of a company with an odd address book. Its real director, Don Channing, is honeymooning on Mars.

Franks makes himself at home in the boss's office. His feet rest on the desk, and he drinks the director's Scotch. The liquor hides in a filing drawer marked S, while drawer B holds beer. His secretary Jeanne teases him for copying Channing's habits. She brings in the mail, including a cheerful postcard from the honeymooners. The banter hints that office comedy will share the stage with space flight.
68670-the-micro-organisms-of-the-soil:
The Micro-Organisms of the Soil is a scientific monograph in the Rothamsted Monographs on Agricultural Science. Sir E John Russell edited the series from Rothamsted, the great English station for farm research. The monograph treats the living population of the soil and its work.

The series introduction explains why such books were needed. In ten years, knowledge of soil and plant relations had grown markedly. The subject now spans physical, biological, and chemical lines at once. Its ramifications had grown too wide for any single textbook. Rothamsted answered with monographs by specialists, this one on the bacteria and other small life of the soil. Soil microbes fix nitrogen, rot humus, and feed crops invisibly. The monograph brought laboratory findings on them into the hands of agricultural readers.
68673-outlaw-jack-or-the-mountain-devil:
Harry Hazard wrote Outlaw Jack, or The Mountain Devil, a pocket novel issued at New York by Beadle and Adams. Hazard had writ Heart Eater, The White Outlaw, and Arkansas Jack, the title page lists. The tale was entered for copyright in 1873 by Frank Starr and Company. Chapter One is named A Blow in the Dark.

Two young men talk by a small white tent half hidden in a grove. Burr tells his mate that a great change has come. The road will be open for them tomorrow, he says, for she is dying. A quavering, pitiful wail from the tent tells the truth plainer than words. A household is broken, with a bereaved husband and daughter left. One of the two men secretly exults that his greatest difficulty is removed. The little valley scene sets love, death, and villainy in motion.
68822-the-tale-of-curly-tail:
Laura Rountree Smith wrote tales of a small dog for Whitman of Chicago, in a set called Just Right Books. Mae Scannell drew the pictures, and the book was copyrighted in 1923. One December day Curly-Tail, the dearest little dog in the world, jumps on his rocking horse and rocks away. He will go to the workshop of Santa Claus, to look for the old parrot.

He rocks all day and sleeps in a cave in the woods. Next morning he has lost the right path, and says so in rhyme. Then comes the patter of small feet down the path. The fourteen little darling dogs are trooping to meet him, and all shout that the lost is found. The chapters ahead hold a happy new year, table manners, and a cookie dog. A circus day parade and garden days fill the rest, with verses sprinkled through.
6905-the-boy-aviators-in-africa-or-an-ae:
Captain Wilbur Lawton sends his boy aviators to Africa on an aerial ivory trail, opening with a reunion and a cache of stolen ivory. Harry, Billy Barnes the reporter, and their chums pack, quarrel, and joke as they set out, warned to be serious about the work ahead. The contents promise a witch doctor, a pool of death, a traitor in camp, and a battle in the air.

Slave traders, gorillas with an aerial tow line, a rogue elephant, and an Arab chief test the boys in turn. Friends in need, a smoke reader, and a rescue by aeroplane carry the tale toward its close aboard the Brigand. Lawton keeps the tone brisk and boyish, with flight as the answer to nearly every peril on the ground.
6906-the-lost-trail:
Edward Ellis opens this frontier tale in early spring, with Jack Carleton, a sturdy youth of seventeen, following a clear trail through western Kentucky toward the Mississippi. Mile by mile he tracks the spaced marks, until an enemy in a tree and a rifle shot break the quiet. Chapters carry him to the river bank, a visitor from the far shore, and nights around the camp fire.

Deerfoot, the skilled woodsman of the chapter titles, shapes much of the action, from a surprised fisherman to maneuvers, messages, and a fort in the trees. The tale moves through pursuits, wigwams, and turning tables, with a stranger, a smoke signal, and a farewell at the close. It is a brisk story of trail craft and nerve.
69341-bonanza-a-story-of-the-gold-trail:
William MacLeod Raine writes a Western in Bonanza, a story of the gold trail copyrighted in 1921 and 1926 and published at New York by Grosset and Dunlap. A prefatory poem toasts the giants who journeyed westward, felled the forests and built towns where the manzanita grows. The chapters open with a Pony Express rider and a cry of Hurrah for Washoe.

Scot McClintock and his son Hugh carry much of the action, through a night ride, a till tapping, a knife with fourteen notches and a blizzard. Vicky tells secrets, the Stranglers appear, and a killer strikes before Hugh hits the trail again.
69429-perch-of-the-devil:
Perch of the Devil is a novel by Gertrude Atherton, published in New York in nineteen fourteen. The hosted copy is a fourth printing of August that year. Atherton dedicates it to two men of Helena, Montana, named on the dedication page. Part one opens on a ranch in a high Montana valley under bright mountains.

Gregory Compton calls them the shining mountains, the name Indians gave them before the white man came, he says. His wife yawns at the phrase and wishes they shone inside, a crack that sets the marriage tone. Mines, money, and a restless wife fill a Montana tale. Atherton knew the West and wrote its new rich with a sharp eye.
69490-the-wood-king-or-daniel-boone-s-la:
Jos E Badger Jr wrote a pocket novel entered for copyright in 1878 by Beadle and Adams, subtitled a romance of the Osage country. Badger had written The Texas Hawks, The Florida Scout, and other pocket novels. Rifle shots open the tale, faint and far away across the eastern forest. A hunter crossing the Osage River at a ford stops midstream to listen.

Yells follow, like a cur dog in pursuit, which mark Indians closing on a fleeing foe. The hunter knows that sound from half a century of frontier life. He is old, with snowy locks under a skin cap, yet light and firm of step. Daniel Boone's last trail gives the story its frame.
6979-the-little-regiment-and-other-episo:
Stephen Crane gathers Civil War episodes here, led by The Little Regiment, with Three Miraculous Soldiers, A Mystery of Heroism, An Indiana Campaign, A Grey Sleeve, and The Veteran. The title story opens in fog, where a column's heavy overcoats take a pale blue hue and the regiment seems a long low shadow in the mist. Above the thick ranks a muttering, part grumble and part joke, blends into the voice of the column.

Across a little river a town looms spectral on grey cloud masses, while guns on the northern bank have battered a belfry into dim sight. Crane writes war as men feel it, in color, sound, and fear, rather than as generals plan it. The stories that follow keep that hard, close focus on soldiers under fire.
69946-the-wolf-trail:
Roger Pocock's adventure novel The Wolf Trail was published by Appleton and Company in New York in 1923. It opens in the Fox under the Hill, a tavern on London River. There the publican Fright serves mulled ale called dogsnose to a mixed company.

Among them is Bill, the bargee's eighteen-year-old son, mending a sea boot. A light-fingered guest waits for a boat out of reach of the magistrates. The contents promise the voyage of the Beaver, British Oregon, Kootenay, the Ghost Trail and Rising Wolf. The story travels from the Thames-side bar parlour to the fur country of the Canadian west.
70101-apache-devil:
Apache Devil is a western novel by Edgar Rice Burroughs, first published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap in 1933. The story follows Shoz-Dijiji, called the Black Bear, a young war chief of the Be-don-ko-he Apaches, through the last campaigns of Geronimo's people.

The opening chapter, Geronimo Goes Out, shows a rain dance led by the medicine man Nan-ta-do-tash under a full moon. Contents move through spoils of war, the war trail, Geronimo and Crook, a chapter offering two thousand dollars for a head, and Skeleton Canyon. Gian-nah-tah, Shoz-Dijiji's friend since boyhood, stands beside him on raids against the soldiers. Burroughs, famous for Tarzan, here writes the Apache wars from the Apache side.
70265-the-pot-of-basil:
The Pot of Basil is a novel by Bernard Capes, printed in 1913. Constable of London brought it out that year. Capes had writ A Jay of Italy and Bag and Baggage before. A note explains the tale grows from a legend in new memoirs. That legend stood first made public there.

Twenty-nine chapters run from the Nixie to a close called At Rest. Aquaviva, the compact, and love's ambassador fill the early Italian tale. Il Trovatore, love-in-a-mist, and correspondence carry the romance forward slowly. The decoy, the orange grove, and sweet basil give the title its scene. Paolo and Francesca lend their names to a chapter of lovers. A bolt from the blue and the lost presence darken the middle. Fair Isabel, poor simple Isabel, heads the tale in a quoted line. Colorno, the petty Versailles of Parma, opens on a hot day.
70379-oil:
Upton Sinclair wrote Oil, a novel published by himself at Pasadena. Rights were held in 1926 and 1927 by Sinclair in two countries. He had written The Jungle and The Brass Check before it. A foreword asks the reader to think of a pack of cards. Shuffle the cards, and deal a new round of poker hands, he says.

The hands differ in every way, yet it is the same pack and game. So with this novel, a picture of life in Southern California. Sinclair observed that life during eleven years of residence there. The picture is the truth, and its mass of detail exists, he holds. But names, places, dates, and episodes have been dealt over again. Only three presidents of the past fifteen years can be recognized, he says. Hunting oil magnates and picture stars in it wastes the reader's time.
70683-the-doom-trail:
The Doom Trail is a historical novel by Arthur Howden Smith. Brentano's published the book at New York in 1922, from magazine rights of the year before. Smith had written Spears of Destiny and other adventure tales. The contents run to thirty chapters, from a fray in a London lane to the barring of the Doom Trail.

A prologue speaks in the voice of the People of the Long House. The speaker offers the reader a place at the council fire and a belt in token of straight words. He mourns that his people are scattered and their villages replaced by white towns. The roads of the white man have wiped out the old war trails. The novel then turns to traders, governors, and frontier war. Chapters promise councils, a moon feast, and an appeal to the Long House.
70899-medusa-s-coil:
Medusa's Coil, by Bishop, author of The Curse of Yig, is a novelette of horror taken from Weird Tales of January 1939. A headnote calls it a powerful tale of brooding horror that deepens to the final catastrophe.

The narrator drives toward Cape Girardeau through unfamiliar country, in the late afternoon light. He needs directions before night, and dreads the bleak southern Missouri lowlands after dark. November cold threatens his open roadster, and black clouds mass on the horizon. At last he spies a roof among trees near a small river. A ruined stone gateway, choked with vines and undergrowth, marks the drive. He parks the car and walks the brush grown path. The house ahead is a wooden plantation house of the early nineteenth century pattern: two and a half stories, and a great Ionic portico whose pillars reach to the attic.
70977-good-for-evil:
Good for Evil, or Rose Cottage, is a moral tale for the young by Leslie, in a run of lake named tales. A line from a letter of Peter heads the book: render not ill for ill, nor rail for rail, but on the far side bless. It came out at Boston in the late eighteen sixties.

Its rights were set in law that year by its house. Its parts open with law students, then a trip home and the greet at the door. Take time by the lock of hair, a sly old saw made a part name, shows its cast. Rush as foe to calm thought, word from the west, broke vows, and thoughts laid bare fill the first run.
71190-brought-out-of-peril:
Brought Out of Peril is a story book for the young by Emma Leslie, issued in London by the Religious Tract Society. The hosted copy is a third impression, and Leslie's other tales are listed on the title page. A contents list of more than nineteen chapters maps the plot. A girl named Fanny stands at the centre of the tale.

Chapter heads trace Fanny's first holiday, a watch that matters to the plot, and friends in need. A renovated home, a terrible blow, and a mother's quest all mark turns in the story. Sunday scenes and new situations point to the moral tone of Tract Society fiction. Peril and rescue carry a clear lesson for young readers.
71261-the-white-mail:
Cy Warman wrote a railroad tale of a section boss's son and his rise. Charles Scribner's Sons held the rights in New York in 1899. Twenty-four chapters run from a watchman's passing to over the big bridge. The book is given to Bryan Warman with a father's love.

Denis McGuire, section boss at Lick Skillet, can neither read nor write. His son Tommy flags the White Mail and learns telegraphy in the tale. Floods, hold-ups, Sioux, and snowbound trains crowd the boy's road up. Rail fans gain a warm, brisk tale of the line in its rough years.
71367-poppy-ott-and-the-galloping-snail:
Leo Edwards wrote Poppy Ott and the Galloping Snail for Grosset and Dunlap of New York in 1927. Bert Salg drew the pictures. The book belongs to Edwards's Poppy Ott series for boys. Its narrator is Jerry Todd, who also stars in a series of his own.

Jerry opens the tale worn out on a sun-baked highway. He kicks off his shoes, cools his blistered feet, and begs Poppy for ice cream. Home is Tutter, Illinois, which Jerry calls the peachiest small town in the state. The chapter list promises a house of mystery and a spotted gander. A ghost in the kitchen, a runaway, and a diary in a clock follow. Quarantine and a scream in the night close the list of troubles.
72186-westy-martin-on-the-santa-fe-trail:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote Westy Martin on the Santa Fe Trail, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1926. Fitzhugh also wrote the Tom Slade, Roy Blakeley, and Pee-Wee Harris books. The volume carries the approval of the Boy Scouts of America, and Richard Holberg drew the pictures.

Westy travels the old Santa Fe Trail with his friend Rip and a girl named Lola. The chapter list promises a legend of Death River, a lake bewitched, and pages out of the past. The party is lost, short of water, and in despair before a scout with wings and a rescue turn the tale. Old scouts, flames, and a trust well kept carry the story home. Fitzhugh blends trail history with scout adventure.
72611-black-april:
Black April, by Julia Peterkin, is a novel of Black farm life. Bobbs Merrill first issued it, with rights held in nineteen twenty seven. Grosset and Dunlap reissued the book by arrangement with that house. Peterkin gives the book to Julius Mood on its dedication page.

Chapters trace April through son, kin, church, field work, and hog killing. The tale opens at dusk on Sandy Island, by a log cabin. Fire glow pours from the open door under moss hung oaks. A gaunt old Black man strides up from the river path. A moan from inside makes his broad hands clench in dread.
72778-a-history-of-the-brazil:
A History of the Brazil is a work by James Henderson, lately from South America. Its title states its scope: the geography, commerce, colonization, and first inhabitants of that land. The book came out in London in 1821, printed for the author and sold by Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown. It holds twenty-eight plates and two maps. A plate shows Don John VI, King of Portugal and Brazil, with his court at Rio de Janeiro.

The book is given to the Lord Viscount Lowther. The dedication opens with a word on the writer's place. Were the author a well-known and praised member of the world of letters, the page runs, he would still be glad of the leave to give his work to that lord. The history is an English account of Brazil in the years of its last days as a Portuguese colony.
73207-the-morgan-trail:
Tuttle wrote The Morgan Trail, a Hashknife Hartley tale put out by Houghton Mifflin in 1928. The book opens with Rex Morgan, a young man of twenty, back from the funeral of his mother. He sits on the porch of the small house that was his home at Northport, in California. It strikes him that he is all alone in the world, with no kin he has ever heard named.

From that low start, the tale moves to work, fights, and range law. Chapters bring fighting nesters, a deadline, an empty safe, and a man in a black mask. Hashknife and his mate Sleepy drift in to stand by Rex. A rug and the smoke of a forty-five play a part. The book gives a fast West tale of loss, grit, and help.
7346-among-malay-pirates-a-tale-of-adven:
G. A. Henty's Among Malay Pirates opens with Harry Parkhurst, a midshipman of sixteen, leaning on the rail of Her Majesty's gunboat Serpent with his chum Dick Balderson, staring gloomily at a turbid stream. One day is just like another, Harry complains. Perspiration runs from morning to night, mist lies on the water, and only a run out every three or four days brings fresh air, lest fever eat them up.

Pirates soon break the dull routine, and the gunboat's boys face adventure and peril in Malay waters. Henty writes brisk naval adventure, with heat, boredom, and sudden action in equal share. Young readers get a sea tale where patience snaps into danger without warning.
73490-the-blowing-away-of-mr-bushy-tail:
Edith Davidson wrote The Blowing Away of Mr. Bushy Tail, a story for children published in New York by Duffield and Company in 1910. Clara Atwood drew the pictures. Davidson dedicated the book to her kind hostess at Highwood, in whose house it was written.

The Bushy Tails are squirrels, and the winter has been hard. Food runs low, and the family of four moves into Grandmother Chipmunk's house tree to escape the wind and snow, though the rooms are small and Grandmother snores. The chapters speak in nursery rhyme lines and send Mr. Bushy Tail tobogganing and then off on the wings of the North Wind. He reaches the top of the South Pole, meets a quilly acquaintance, and hears the snortling of the Ring-Tailed Snorter. The gentle South Wind brings the close. Young readers get a winter adventure in a tree.
73521-opening-the-iron-trail:
Edwin Sabin wrote Opening the Iron Trail, or Terry as a U-Pay man, copyrighted in New York in 1919. A front picture shows the wedding of the rails. Sabin's books list puts this tale in his Great West series, beside the Pike's Peak rush and the overland stage. A song of the U-Pay men, all drill and work with no sugar in the tea, stands on the title page.

A note to the reader sets the facts the tale is built on. Fifty years before, at noon on May 10, 1869, the last rails of the Pacific Railway were laid at Promontory Point, Utah. The engines of the Union Pacific and the Central Pacific touched noses there. The Union Pacific had built over a thousand miles of track in three years from Omaha. The Central Pacific had built over six hundred from Sacramento.
73765-count-luckner-the-sea-devil:
Count Luckner, the Sea Devil, by Lowell Thomas, was copyright in 1927, with pictures from photographs. Its front page calls Count Felix von Luckner the most romantic and strange figure of the World War. Thomas first meets him on a flying field in central Europe, on a trip by air from London toward Moscow.

Thirty chapters trace the count from boy runaway to sea raider. Early chapters tell of Australia, wrestling, and a tragic cruise. Later chapters tell of a fake crew, a run through the British blockade, and ships taken at sea. The tale ends with shipwreck, an open boat, capture at Wakaya, and escape from New Zealand. Readers get a fast life of a sail raider told as high adventure.
74333-hunting-a-home-in-brazil:
Hunting a Home in Brazil was written by J McF Gaston, a doctor of Columbia, South Carolina, who had served as a surgeon in the Confederate Army. King and Baird printed the book in Philadelphia in 1867. Its full title promises the agricultural resources and other characteristics of the country, with the manners and customs of its people.

The book grew out of an extended tour through central Brazil, made with ample help from the imperial authorities. Gaston kept a daily record for personal friends, then printed it for the many others who might seek a home in a land of vast resources. He reports that all the requisites of a desirable home are found in Brazil, and offers his data on soil, climate, people, and government as the grounds for judging.
74774-people-of-the-veil:
People of the Veil, by Francis Rennell Rodd, came out from Macmillan in London in 1926. The book gives an account of the wandering Tuareg tribes of the central Sahara. Their home is the mountains of Air, or Asben, in the great desert.

Rodd treats their habits, their social order, and their history across the whole book. A plate of Agellal village and its mountains fronts the volume. He thanks the governor of Nigeria and the French ministry of colonies for help on the road. Angus Buchanan shared the journey with him. An appendix gives a table of the kings of Agades, drawn from a paper by Palmer of Northern Nigeria. Rodd also thanks Hogarth, who read his draft and shaped its final form.
7537-shallow-soil:
Knut Hamsun, the Norwegian novelist who would win the Nobel Prize, writes of a land and a boy shaped by it. This is the authorized translation by Carl Christian Hyllested. The translator's preface recalls the stir of Hamsun's first autobiographical chapters. They appeared in a Danish magazine in the autumn of 1888, when Ibsen, Björnson, Brandes, and Strindberg stood at the height of their European fame.

The world of the novel is Norway's rugged coast, a drama in granite flung far into the Arctic night. There a taciturn, peculiar lad grows up inured to hardship and danger, in close communion with nature, dreaming through the endless northern twilight and reveling through the brief, intense summer. Shallow Soil gives English readers Hamsun's northern ground: hard, beautiful, and unforgiving.
75697-the-end-of-the-trail:
The End of the Trail tells of the far West from New Mexico to British Columbia. Powell wrote it after The Last Frontier and Gentlemen Rovers. Scribner's Sons brought the book out in New York in 1914. Forty-eight full-page pictures and a map back the long road tale. He gives the book to Albert Kuhn, his friend and fellow rover.

Fifteen chapters run from sun and sand lands to the half-unrolled map. Skylanders, gold on trees, and the coast of fairyland fill the road north. The Valley of Heart's Delight and the modern Argonauts come midway. Oregon, a frontier Arcady, and breaking the wilderness fill the late list. Rivets of empire get clinched before the back of beyond closes it. Photographs show Santa Fé, Acoma, and desert dawns in New Mexico. Powell writes as a man who rode the ground he describes.
75760-the-house-of-evil:
William Le Queux published his novel The House of Evil with Ward, Lock at London and Melbourne in 1927. Twenty-four chapters carry the tale, listed by number alone. Chapter one strolls the Promenade des Anglais at Nice with two old school friends. Hugh Craig, a diplomat on holiday, keeps dining out and hiding his errands.

Leonard Lydon teases Craig for growing as close as an oyster. Craig is the youngest son of Viscount Clandon, bred at Harrow and Balliol for state service. Lydon, a Liverpool merchant's son, works as chief engineer for a wireless firm after Admiralty war service. Friendship, money, and radio skill set the board. Le Queux deals out a Riviera mystery in his brisk house style.
75998-daredevil:
Daredevil is a crime novel by Leslie Charteris, copyrighted in 1929. A line at the front states its ending in advance. The day Captain Arden put on his steel waistcoat, it says, the menace of the Alpha Triangle was forever quelled.

The first chapter belongs to Susan Hawthorne instead. Her father, old Smiler Hawthorne, has died after a life of globe-trotting. He leaves her his name and thirty pounds. The rest vanished a week earlier with the promoter of a diamond field that held no diamonds. Susan, not one to look for charity, goes to Lord Hannassay. The contents promise the machinery of the thriller around her. Storm is introduced, goes gunning, and fights the last round. Charteris mixes the orphan's plight with the fight against the Triangle, in his brisk early manner.
76378-the-movie-boys-in-peril:
The Movie Boys in Peril, or strenuous days along the Panama Canal, by Victor Appleton, was published by Garden City Publishing Company in 1926, under copyrights of 1915 and 1926. Appleton wrote a shelf of Movie Boys books: in the wild west, in the jungle, and in earthquake land. Blake and Joe, the movie boys, travel to film what other boys only read about.

The tale opens with speed. A big shiny motorcycle swings into the drive of a white farmhouse, and Blake tells Joe it will do better than ninety miles an hour on the level. No mail has come, though a letter from Mr Hadley is overdue, and Joe waits on one from Mabel. Birdie Lee's name teases them both. The chapter is called To the Rescue, and the road south to the canal lies ahead of the boys and their camera.
76531-resist-not-evil:
Clarence S Darrow wrote Resist Not Evil, a sharp attack on force and punishment. Charles H Kerr issued the book in Chicago with a nineteen hundred two copyright. Bible lines on the turned cheek face the title page. Ads call the work a startling charge at the rule of force.

The first chapter asks what the state is by nature. Armies and fleets get two chapters on their aims. Crime and its cure form the heart of the book. Darrow asks if pain can mend a wrong at all. He doubts that men can judge each other justly. Judges, codes, and the mills of law all face his doubt. His close pleads for kind cure in place of revenge.
76683-a-summer-journey-to-brazil:
Alice Humphrey wrote this travel book, A Summer Journey to Brazil, printed at New York and London in 1900. Two mottoes head it. One says Brazil is an unknown land to the general American public, less known than Asia or the North Pole. The other quotes a poem of Dickinson, refused with a smile by a mighty merchant. Contents plot a summer's route south.
