From New York the chapters run to Lisbon, then two weeks in tropical seas, and Pernambuco. Two beautiful bays, Petropolis, Santos and some Brazilians, and the city of São Paulo follow, before the homeward bound. An appendix takes up schools, churches, facts about Brazil, and a naval revolt ended under American protection. Pictures show Lisbon, Rio's docks, an alley of palms, and the picking, washing, and drying of coffee.
77939-two-way-trail:
Clay Perry wrote this Alaska story, subtitled a romance of Alaska, treasure house of strange stories of men and women and life in the raw. It opens in camp almost one hundred miles above Dawson, with the mercury at fifty below.

The old sourdough Shorty Freem lights his cracked corncob with a splinter, scorching his thumb. Beside him, Gresham, a newspaperman sent north to find human color along the old gold trails, listens anxiously. The third man, Hartwell, sits hooded in his robes, young eyes in a snow-white-haired face, his own story untold. Shorty begins a tale of Dawson in the winter of the food panic. The dogs burrow in the snow bank as the arctic night closes down. Readers get a Yukon frame tale at fifty below.
78606-say-it-with-bricks-say-it-with-oil:
Two comic pieces share one small book printed at New York in 1923. Nina Wilcox Putnam writes a few remarks about husbands in the first half. Ring Lardner answers in kind on oil in the second. Putnam gives her half to the man who gave her the idea.

She tells how her publisher coaxed the piece from her. He asked what she thought of husbands, and she said it could not be printed. He offered cash, and her resolve wavered. Having had two husbands, and been a widow between, she held herself fit for the theme. At last she agrees to tell not what she thinks, but what she knows of the breed.
79360-the-planet-of-peril:
Otis Adelbert Kline wrote The Planet of Peril, a tale run in Argosy All-Story Weekly across July and August 1929. Its hero is Robert Grandon, a rich young man of Chicago, bored by opera, dinners, and his doting aunt's mansion on Sheridan Road.

In the smoking room a smiling stranger offers Grandon a cigarette from the far side of the case. Grandon grows drowsy, slumps, and is carried out as if faint. The magazine's note gives the game away: he wakes to wild adventure on cloud wrapped Venus. Sword play and peril wait on that weird planet.
79376-the-voice-of-el-lil:
The Voice of El-Lil is a tale by Robert Howard, printed in Oriental Stories in October and November 1930. Its note sets the scene: in the heart of African Somaliland stood an eastern city carried over from the valley of the Tigris and Euphrates, a modern tale of ancient Sumeria. The story is told by a drifter in the port of Maskat.

Maskat, the narrator says, shelters wanderers of many nations, and its bazar rings with the tongues of half the Orient. In a bar there, the sound of a Chinese gong makes the big Englishman beside him start and spill his drink. The man is a born fighter of old Anglo-Saxon stock, and he is in a mood to talk.
79429-applause-mail:
Oney Fred Sweet wrote Applause Mail, a broadcasting story that could not possibly have been written ten years before, the caption boasts. Betty Parsons advises persons craving a tryout on station WMQZ that program director Henri Salzman will be in after three o'clock. She could say only that and fulfil her duty at the desk.

But something attractive marks the aspiring young man across the railing, instrument case under his arm, hardly the musician type. Plenty of outdoors and athletics stand in his background, Betty judges with six months of office wisdom. Whether he makes good will depend on the applause mail, she warns him kindly. Fans rave over announcer Bert Hall, married and balding. Radio romance follows.
79503-sword-play-based-upon-the-french-s:
Sword Play is a fencing manual based on the French school of the foil, by two Breckinridges. Father and son wrote it together and published it through Barnes in New York. Rights are dated nineteen forty one on the copyright page of the book. The pair dedicate it to their old master, Francois Darrieulat of Dax.

Darrieulat taught at clubs in Washington, at the Naval Academy, and at Cornell. He twice coached American Olympic fencing teams in his long career. Seven chapters run from first steps to the duelling sword and the saber. Guard, advance, retreat, thrust, and lunge fill the opening chapter on basics. Defence, attack, feints, and the one two follow in the second chapter. Irregular practices, the bout, exercises, and class teaching close the course.
896-the-jubilee-of-the-constitution-deli:
John Quincy Adams delivered this oration on 30 April 1839, before the New York Historical Society, to mark the jubilee of the Constitution. Fifty years after Washington's first inauguration, Adams asks his fellow citizens to recall the founding act, its authors, and the Union it made, and to weigh what it still demands.

Adams speaks as a former president and a son of a founder, with learning and moral gravity. His oration praises the Constitution as a living bond, not a dead letter, and warns against forgetting its spirit. The text is a key document of American civic oratory, and of Adams's late public voice.
9857-the-long-labrador-trail:
Dillon Wallace wrote The Long Labrador Trail in 1917, a true tale of travel through Labrador's wilds. Wallace, famed for The Lure of the Labrador Wild, dedicates the book to his wife's memory. Chapters follow the voice of the wilderness, the old Indian trail, and Lake Nipishish, toward Seal Lake and Michikamau. A parting, a northern divide, and disaster in the rapids follow.

Later chapters bring tidewater posts, Eskimo camps, Arctic ice, and a sledge journey across the barrens. Wallace writes with hardy, plain detail. A reader gets a gripping northern travel book, rich in trails, lakes, and the endurance of men and dogs.
9932-the-last-trail:
Zane Grey's 1909 frontier novel opens at dusk in the wild Ohio valley, where a traveler on the river trail hopes to reach Fort Henry that night. His guide has abandoned him, his teamster is new to the frontier, and the forest trail grows hard to follow.

From that anxious start, Grey builds a story of wilderness travel, Indian danger, and frontier courage, in the land of his earlier border tales. His eye for rivers, forests, and lonely trails gives the book its force. Readers get a classic western of the Ohio country, when the frontier was still raw and thinly held.
a-holiday-in-the-happy-valley-with-pen-a: Thomas Robert Swinburne takes a holiday in the happy valley with pen and pencil. His illustrated journey visits Srinagar, the Jhelum, the Dal Lake, and Udaipur in Kashmir. Colored illustrations show byways, bunds, boats, and mountain tarns. Swinburne writes and draws a traveler's portrait of Kashmir in early spring. The pen and pencil work makes Kashmir feel near and real.
a-new-conscience-and-an-ancient-evil: Jane Addams examines the ancient evil of her title, the traffic in women that large cities preferred not to name, in this Hull House study. Drawing on material gathered by the Juvenile Protective Association of Chicago, she argues that a new public conscience must replace silence about women cast out as outcasts. She moves through legal enactments, economic conditions, moral education, rescue work, and increased social control as remedies.
among-malay-pirates-a-tale-of-adventure-:
G. A. Henty wrote Among Malay Pirates as a tale of adventure and peril for boy readers, and it opens aboard Her Majesty's gunboat Serpent in hot, feverish river country. Midshipmen Harry Parkhurst and Dick Balderson, both about sixteen, are bored with anchor duty and longing for something to happen among the passing canoes and dhows.

Something does: the river world they watch, of traders, chiefs, and pirate crews, turns dangerous, and the boys are drawn into captures, escapes, and fighting up-country. Henty mixes naval routine, local color as his age saw it, and steady doses of peril to keep his young heroes earning their keep. It is empire-era adventure fiction in his standard, much-reprinted mould.
basil:
Wilkie Collins published Basil in 1852, his second novel, dedicated to his friend Charles James Ward. Collins founded the story, he says, on a main event drawn from real life, and cast it in three parts with letters in conclusion. Basil, a younger son of wealth, falls for Margaret, a linen-draper's daughter, and marries her in secret under a year's probation.

The middle turns on overhearing: Basil, in the garden at North Villa, catches Margaret and her mother plotting deceit for the sake of a new dress. Faces recur in fevered dreams — a figure on a doorstep disclosed by lightning as frightful reality. Collins builds the sensation novel's machinery here early: class shame, a villainous seducer waiting offstage, and a hero whose own confession supplies the horror.
beyond-good-and-evil:
Friedrich Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil appears here in the English translation by Helen Zimmern. Nietzsche opens with a preface mocking dogmatic philosophers, thinkers who claim final systems of truth. He calls Plato's pure spirit and absolute good a noble error now happily outgrown. The book that follows is restless, witty, and deliberately unsettling.

Nine chapters move from the prejudices of philosophers to the free spirit and the religious mood. A chapter of aphorisms, short sharp sayings, interrupts the argument. Later parts give a natural history of morals, reflections on scholars, and portraits of peoples and countries. The final chapter asks what nobility means. Nietzsche urges readers to question herd morality, the values of the crowd, and to create values of their own.
britannica-1911-abigail: Abigail is the subject of a short Bible entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, read here inside a shared chunk of text. The entry gives the Hebrew name's sense as perhaps father is joy. In the Bible it names the wife of Nabal the Carmelite, who became David's wife on Nabal's death. Her son by David appears as Chileab, Daluyah, or Daniel across the texts. A sister of David bore the name as well. Common speech took abigail as a word for a waiting-woman.
britannica-1911-alguazil:
Readers of Spanish stories and plays often meet an alguazil, an officer whose standing fell sharply over time. The name joins the Arabic article al to the word for a vizier, or chief minister. Early in Spain such a man could judge cases or even govern a town or fortress. That long slide, from high office to humble duty, is the heart of the short entry.

Later the post shrank. An alguazil became a court officer who served writs and did some police work, though he still outranked the corchete, the catch-poll who made arrests. Market towns also gave the title to men who checked weights and measures, along with like officials.
britannica-1911-arcueil:
Arcueil is a town in northern France, south of Paris on the Bièvre river. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica derives its name from a Roman aqueduct once there. Traces of that old work still stood when the entry was made. A church built from the thirteenth to fifteenth century marks the town center.

Water works define the place more than any other feature. In the early sixteen hundreds a long bridge aqueduct was built to Paris. A still longer one was stacked above it in later years. Together they rose about one hundred thirty five feet high. Bleaching, leather work, and stone quarries gave local jobs.
britannica-1911-ardebil:
Ardebil is a town in north west Persia, in the province of Azerbaijan. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it on a rich plain at 4,500 feet. The Baluk Su river runs past the town. Mount Savelan, a cone of old lava, bounds the plain to the west. About ten thousand people lived there at the time. Trade in Armenian hands still mattered, the entry says. Much of it was transit trade between Russia and Persia.

Inside the town stand famed shrines and tombs. They honour Shaikh Safi and his heir Shah Ismail the First. Ismail founded the Safavi line and ruled as the first Shiah shah of Persia. In past ages the town drew merchants from Europe and China. Goods from central Asia and India passed through it toward Europe. Since the 1500s, crowds of pilgrims have come for the shrine of Shaikh Safi.
britannica-1911-aulic-council:
The Aulic Council, a chief body of the Holy Roman Empire, is explained in a 1911 Britannica article. It was first meant for rule work but acted chiefly as a court. It worked from 1497 to 1806. In early times each emperor had his own loose band of advisers.

In the 1300s a set council arose, with paid members who held their posts for good. Many were trained in law. The body ran much of the rule of the realm and heard pleas sent to the king. Its true start, the piece says, came with Maximilian the First in 1497 to 1498. He set up the council with two sister bodies, one for funds and one for state papers.
britannica-1911-aventail: Aventail, also spelled Avantaille, was the mouthpiece of an old-fashioned helmet, made movable so the wearer could admit air. The word comes from Old French esventail, traced to a Latin word for an air-hole. The short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry gives only this meaning, linking the name, the part of the helmet at the mouth, and its use for breathing.
britannica-1911-bail:
Bail, in English common law, is the freeing of a person arrested or jailed. The case may be civil or criminal. Surety is taken for his appearance on a set day at a set place. The sureties are themselves called bail, since the prisoner passes into their custody and they may surrender him back to court.

Rules vary by charge. Bail is a right in summary cases and in most misdemeanours. Listed exceptions include perjury and riot. In treason, only a secretary of state or the king's bench can grant it. For felony there is no right: judges weigh the evidence, the accused's position, the likely punishment, and the chance of flight. The Bail Act of 1898 let magistrates drop sureties where justice would not suffer.
britannica-1911-bakunin-mikhail:
Bakunin, Mikhail (1814-1876), was a Russian anarchist. An aristocratic Tver family bore him. He served as an Imperial Guard officer. Polish service showed him despotism's methods. Disgust made him resign his commission. Germany and Hegel claimed him next.

In Paris Bakunin met Proudhon and George Sand. Polish exiles became his acquaintances there. Switzerland gave him a base for agitation. Russia ordered him home in vain. His property was confiscated for refusal. A violent tirade expelled him from France in 1848. Dresden's 1849 rising brought a death sentence. Commutation changed it to life imprisonment. Russian prisons and Siberian exile followed. He escaped through Japan and America in 1861. England received him that year. In 1869 he founded the Social Democratic Alliance. The International expelled him in 1872. Marx's party outvoted him at the Hague.
britannica-1911-bambino-il:
Il Bambino, Italian for the Babe, is the name given in art to the image of the infant Jesus in swaddling clothes. Such images are common in Roman Catholic churches. The 1911 Britannica entry is a short one, and it centres on the most famous case of all.

That case is the Santissimo Bambino of the church of Ara Coeli at Rome, held to work miracles. Its festival is kept on the feast of the Epiphany, on 6 January. Beyond naming the type of image and its Roman example, the entry adds little, so readers get a definition, a location, and a feast day, and no more.
britannica-1911-baudry-of-bourgueil:
Baudry, also called Balderich, of Bourgueil (1046 or 1047–1130) was a French churchman, historian, and poet, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Meung-sur-Loire, he entered the Benedictine abbey of Bourgueil and became its abbot in 1079, though his time went more to letters than to office. Failing to win Orleans in 1097, he became archbishop of Dol in 1107.

Office and writing pull the life two ways. The see of Dol was of doubtful rank, so Baudry is called both archbishop and bishop. He tried to school the untaught people of Brittany, failed, and gave up. He sat in councils at the Lateran and at Reims, spent two years in England, then left his diocese to itself, living mostly in Normandy. His prose counts for more than his weak Latin poems. Chief is his Historiae Hierosolymitanae, a history of the First Crusade.
britannica-1911-bayard-pierre-terrail:
Pierre Terrail, seigneur de Bayard (1473–1524), a French soldier, is the hero of a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He came of a noble house in Dauphiné whose heads had fallen in battle for two centuries past. As a page to the duke of Savoy he caught the eye of Charles VIII of France, who took him into the royal train in 1487. Young Bayard stood out for his looks, manners, and skill in the tilt-yard.

Deeds in Italy made the legend.  Chasing foes into Milan alone, he was captured, but Sforza freed him without ransom. The tale most told of him says he held the bridge of the Garigliano alone against some 200 Spaniards. Pope Julius II tried in vain to hire him away. The entry shows a knight whose restless energy and valour ran through all the Italian wars of his age.
britannica-1911-blackmail:
Blackmail is treated here as a word with three distinct uses in English law over time. The entry first tests where the second half of the word came from, linking it to mail, meaning rent or tribute, rather than to a small copper coin. Each sense is then set out in turn.

At first blackmail meant rent paid in labour, grain, or base metal rather than silver. In the northern counties it later meant tribute paid to freebooters so farms would be left alone, made a felony by a law of 1601. In modern use it means getting money or goods by threats of exposure, libel, or prosecution. Readers are sent on to the entries on coercion and extortion.
britannica-1911-boil:
Boil, in medicine, is a hard, swelling sore of the skin that fills with pus and forms a core of dead tissue. The entry lays the cause to a germ named Staphylococcus pyogenes. Boils came most often on young people whose blood was out of order, or as a side trouble in some diseases.

Treatment, as set out here, worked to bring the sore out, help it empty with the lancet, and clear the whole system. The word is also used in the Bible and in street speech for many kinds of ulcer. Named tropical forms end the account: the Aleppo boil, Delhi boil, and Biskra button, face ulcers tied to a small parasite.
britannica-1911-bronzino-il:
Bronzino, Il, is the name given to Angelo Allori (1502–1572), a Florentine painter. He became the favourite pupil of Jacopo da Pontormo, the master whose manner shaped his art. Portrait painting made his reputation, and the sitters named reach to the summit of Italian letters.

He painted portraits of some of the most famous men of his day, among them Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio, the three crowns of early Italian writing as the entry presents them. Most of his best works remain in Florence, but examples hang in the National Gallery in London and elsewhere. The notice is very short, giving name, dates, master, sitters and where the work can be seen, and nothing more.
britannica-1911-castor-oil:
Castor oil is the fixed oil got from the seeds of the castor oil plant, Ricinus communis, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. The plant is a native of tropical Africa, now grown in most warm lands. It runs from a shrub to a tree of 30 or 40 feet, with great palm-shaped leaves that make it a garden ornament.

Its fruit is a three-celled pod with soft prickles, each cell holding one marbled seed. The seeds carry a poison so strong that three have been known to kill a grown man. Oil is won by pressing or by boiling, the boiling way being common in India, where the cheap oil lights homes. Calcutta oil for Europe is pressed from crushed seed, heated with water, strained, and bleached in sunlight. Good oil is also made in Italy and in California on a large scale.
britannica-1911-cecil:
Cecil is the name of a great English house traced from plain roots in a 1911 Britannica kin entry. Two lines of the house each hold a high rank in the realm. Lord Burghley, its great founder, sought grand roots for the line. His probe made more than one fine but false tale of its past. His grandfather is the first man of the line who can be proved.

That root stock was a set of small land men on the Welsh border. One of them rose at Stamford as mayor and as a member of the diet. Court posts and land grants from abbey sales built the line wealth. His grandson William Cecil rose by sheer skill in state work. In fifteen seventy one that man was made Lord Burghley by the queen.
britannica-1911-cod-liver-oil:
Cod liver oil is oil drawn from the liver of the common cod. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains how grades are made. Old makers let livers rot in tubs until oil rose. Pale and light brown grades were skimmed from the top.

Heat on the scraps then forced out a black brown oil. Tanners used that coarse grade, while drug sellers took the pale kinds. Modern works steam fresh cleaned livers and keep air away. That method gives the steamed liver oils of trade. Norway leads the trade, with Canada and Iceland also named. Chemists found the oil rich in mixed fats and rare acids. Some of those acids occur nowhere else in the animal world, the entry says.
britannica-1911-codicil: Codicil is the subject of a short law article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a Latin word for a little book or tablet. A codicil is an addition to a will. Through it a person who made a will can add a wish, take back a wish, explain a wish, or change a wish. In English law a codicil must be signed with the same formal steps as a will. Those steps rest on the Wills Act of 1837.
britannica-1911-colza-oil: Colza oil, a non drying oil pressed from the seed of a Brassica plant kin to the Swedish turnip, is described in a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The crop grew widely in France, Belgium, Holland and Germany, and pressing it was a key trade in France most of all. In trade it was classed with rape oil, its close kin. The pale oil has almost no smell, the cake left after pressing made good cattle feed, and the oil served to grease machines and burn in lamps.
britannica-1911-croton-oil:
Croton oil is an oil pressed from the seeds of Croton Tiglium, a tree of India and the Malay Islands, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. The tree stands fifteen to twenty feet high, with spreading branches and oval leaves. Its fruit is a three-cornered capsule about the size of a hazel nut, holding three cells, each with one seed.

The seeds look like those of the castor-oil plant, but their surface is dull brown rather than polished and mottled, a point the article calls of real practical weight. The kernels hold fifty to sixty per cent of oil, won by pressing them, bruised to a pulp, between hot plates. The oil is a clear, sticky liquid with a sharp, lasting taste and a sour reaction, and the article lists the acids it contains.
britannica-1911-faber-basil:
Basil Faber (1520 to about 1576), a Lutheran schoolmaster and church scholar, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Sorau in lower Lusatia, he entered the university at Wittenberg in 1538. He studied there free of charge as a poor student under Melanchthon. Choosing the schoolmaster's trade, he became head of schools at Nordhausen, Tennstadt, Magdeburg, and Quedlinburg in turn.

The article says he was removed from his last post in 1570 as a secret Calvinist. The next year he was made director of the council school at Erfurt, where he stayed until his death. He turned part of Luther's notes on Genesis into print and helped spread Lutheran views in other ways. He wrote for the first four of the Magdeburg Centuries. He is best known for a great storehouse of school learning, printed in 1571.
britannica-1911-franzos-karl-emil:
Karl Emil Franzos (1848-1904), German novelist, was born of Jewish parentage in Russian Podolia on 25 October 1848 and grew up at Czortków in Galicia. After his district-doctor father died early, the boy taught to support himself while preparing for study. He read law at Vienna and Graz, then left the state judicial service for journalism and wide travel.

From 1877 Franzos lived in Vienna, editing a pictured weekly, and in 1887 he moved to Berlin and founded the review Deutsche Dichtung. His story collections Aus Halb-Asien (1876) and Die Juden von Barnow (1877) drew vivid pictures of life in south-eastern Europe. Later novels include Moschko von Parma, Ein Kampf ums Recht, and Judith Trachtenberg. He died in Berlin in January 1904.
britannica-1911-fusel-oil:
Fusel oil, its name taken from a German word for bad spirits, is the oily liquid found in the last portions of the distillate of fermented grain, potatoes or grape marc. Because it boils higher than ethyl alcohol, it collects late in the distillation. Its chief part in potato and grain spirit is isoprimary amyl alcohol, and other alcohols appear in it, along with ethers and fatty acids. The fusel oil of French marc brandy carries normal propyl alcohol, and that of beet molasses carries isoprimary butyl alcohol.

Fusel oil and its chief constituent act as direct nerve poisons. Small doses bring thirst, headache and a furred tongue, while large doses convulse. Rabuteau held that the higher alcohols grow more toxic as their molecular weight and boiling point rise. Richet judged the fusel oil in spirits the chief danger of drinking them, since impure drinks deepen the disorders of alcoholism.
britannica-1911-goltz-bogumil:
Bogumil Goltz (1801–1870) was a German humorist and writer of satire. He was born at Warsaw on 20 March 1801. After school at Marienwerder and Königsberg, he learned farming on an estate near Thorn. In 1821 he entered the university of Breslau to study thought. He soon gave up that path. After a time back in country life, he settled in the small town of Gollub and gave himself to books.

In 1847 Goltz settled at Thorn, the home of Copernicus, where he died in 1870. His name in letters rests most on his Buch der Kindheit of 1847. In that book he gives a sweet picture of his own young years. He writes in the manner of Jean Paul and Stifter, but with a more modern touch of fact. His other works include a life of his youth.
britannica-1911-grenville-sir-bevil:
Sir Bevil Grenville (1596-1643) was a Royalist soldier in the English Civil War, educated at Exeter College, Oxford. The 1911 Britannica entry has him sitting in parliament for Cornwall, then for Launceston. There he backed Sir John Eliot and the opposition, and his closeness to Eliot lasted for life.

Yet in 1639 he appears as a royalist, going to the Scottish War in the train of Charles I. The entry admits the reasons for his change are unknown, but insists his honour was above suspicion. He was, it says, the most generally loved man in Cornwall. At the war's outbreak he proclaimed the king's Commission of Array and turned the county's machinery against his old allies. Under Hopton he fought at Bradock Down. At Stratton, on 16 May 1643, he led one of the storming parties that broke Chudleigh's lines. The article ends with his death in the Cornish campaign.
britannica-1911-hail:
Hail is the subject of a weather entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word has cognate forms across the Teutonic tongues. It names rounded masses or single pellets of ice that fall from the clouds in a shower. True hail has a layered structure at its core.

That structure forms as frozen particles fall into a warm cloud and are then carried up again. Rising warm air lifts them into a cold layer, where a fresh coat of vapour freezes on them. The stone falls again, gains another coat, and is lifted once more. Through that cycle the hailstone grows until it is too heavy to stay aloft.
britannica-1911-hair-tail: The hair-tail is a sea fish with a long band like body that ends in a tail as thin as a thread. The 1911 Britannica entry places it in a broad group of spiny finned fish. Strong, bold teeth fill both of its jaws. Several kinds of the fish are known to science. One kind is common in the warm Atlantic sea, and it not rarely strays north to the shores of the British Isles, far from its home waters.
britannica-1911-holub-emil:
Emil Holub (1847–1902) was a Bohemian traveller in south-central Africa, born at Holitz in 1847. He took his M.D. at Prague University. In 1872 he went to the Kimberley diamond-fields, and money from his surgeon work there funded expeditions into the northern Transvaal, Mashonaland and Bechuanaland to the Victoria Falls. He brought his natural history collections to Europe in 1879 and spread them among over a hundred museums and schools.

In 1883 Holub returned with his wife, meaning to cross the continent to Egypt. In June 1886 the party crossed the Zambezi west of the Falls and explored the little-known country toward the Kafue. Beyond the Kafue the Mashukulumbwe attacked the camp, and he had to turn back. He reached Austria in 1887 with over 13,000 specimens of great scientific interest. His books include Sieben Jahre in Südafrika (1880–1881). He died at Vienna in 1902.
britannica-1911-hubner-emil:
Emil Hubner is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a German classical scholar. He was born at Dusseldorf in 1834. His father, Julius Hubner, was a painter of history scenes. Emil studied at Berlin and at Bonn. He then travelled widely for research on old remains. His trips centred on carved texts from the Roman world.

That travel bore fruit in a string of large works. His books set out the Latin inscriptions of Spain. A like work covered the Latin texts of Britain. He wrote on the archaeology of Spain as well. He also set out the marks of the old Iberian tongue. Two handbooks made him of great use to students. One mapped Latin writing by period, and one listed works on the ancient world.
britannica-1911-jackson-cyril:
Cyril Jackson (1746–1819) was dean of Christ Church, Oxford, born in Yorkshire and schooled at Westminster and Oxford. In 1771 he was chosen to teach the two eldest sons of George III. He lost that post in 1776, most likely through plots in the royal house. He then took holy orders. In 1779 he became a preacher at Lincoln's Inn and a canon of Christ Church.

In 1783 Jackson was chosen dean of Christ Church. His love for the college led him to refuse the bishopric of Oxford in 1799. He also refused the primacy of Ireland in 1800. He took a lead part in the rule of 1802 that set up public tests at Oxford. Apart from that work, he was not to the fore in the affairs of the university. He left his post in 1809 and lived at Felpham in Sussex till his death.
britannica-1911-jebeil:
Jebeil, the ancient Gebal or Byblus, is a town of Syria described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It sits on a slight rise near the sea, about 20 miles north of Beirut. A wall of about a mile and a half rings the town, with square towers at its angles. A castle stands at the south east corner of that wall. Its count is given as 3,000, all of them Moslems.

Broken granite columns in the gardens and ruined houses in the town speak of its former weight. The stele of Jehawmelek, king of Gebal, found there is one of the chief Phoenician monuments known. The small port is near choked with sand and ruins in the present day. The folk of old Gebal were famed as stone cutters and ship builders in their time.
britannica-1911-king-s-evil:
King's Evil is the old name for scrofula, a swelling sickness of the neck. An article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how kings were once thought to cure it by a touch. Only the royal houses of England and France claimed this gift. Both houses linked the gift to the pure oil used at their crowning.

The piece traces the rite from claims about Clovis and Edward the Confessor. It shows that the rite can first be traced in the time of Edward the Third in England. It also tells of the gold touch piece given to each sick person. Later kings used a set form of service for the rite.
britannica-1911-mare-s-tail: Mare tail, in botany, is the popular name for a water herb known in science as Hippuris vulgaris. Its brief plant entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica places it on the margins of lakes and ponds. A stout creeping rootstock under water sends up jointed round stems. Those stems bear many narrow leaves set close in whorls. Tiny greenish flowers grow in the leaf axils. It ranges wide, through arctic and mild zones of the north and again in far south America.
britannica-1911-maude-cyril:
Cyril Maude, an English actor, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in London in eighteen sixty two, he was educated at Charterhouse. He began his stage career in America in eighteen eighty three. From eighteen ninety six he co managed the Haymarket Theatre in London with a partner.

At the Haymarket he became known for quiet, humorous acting in many parts. In nineteen hundred six he went into management on his own. The next year he opened his new theatre, the Playhouse. In eighteen eighty eight he wed the actress Winifred Emery. She had acted with Irving at the Lyceum as a young performer.
britannica-1911-may-phil:
Phil May, an English artist known for his comic drawings, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Leeds in eighteen sixty four, he was the son of an engineer. His father died when he was nine. By age twelve he had begun to earn his own living.

The entry follows his hard youth, from work at a foundry to time on the stage. At about seventeen he went to London with very little money. He slept in parks and streets before he found work in design. He drew for papers in London, then spent three years in Australia with the Sydney Bulletin.
britannica-1911-merthyr-tydfil:
Merthyr Tydfil is a borough and market town of Glamorganshire in south Wales. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it 69,228 people in 1901. It sits in a bleak, hilly region on the river Taff. Its name is said to come from a martyred saint of the fifth century. Bad sanitation once brought severe epidemics there. A pure water supply from the lesser Taff later fixed that.

Iron made the town. Rich ironstone and coal in the district drew the works. Four great ironworks rose there between 1759 and 1782. Dowlais, the earliest, passed to the Guest family as sole owners. Cyfarthfa, started in 1765, went to the Crawshay family in 1794. The Plymouth works changed hands more than once and shut in 1882. For a time Merthyr stood as the chief seat of Welsh iron.
britannica-1911-moretto-il:
Il Moretto, a name that means the Blackamoor, is the title bestowed on Alessandro Bonvicino in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a famed painter of Brescia in the Venetian school, who lived from 1498 to 1554. Born at Rovato in the Brescian lands, he studied first under Fioravante Ferramola of Brescia. Still young, he then passed to Titian in Venice.

His own early method rested on the manner of Titian in natural course. Portrait painting of high grade marked that first phase of his work. Later he conceived a great love for Raphael, though he seems never to have gone to Rome. His style then took a partly Raphaelesque cast in its forms. It stayed novel in its blend of mixed parts all the same. Fine drawing, a rich but not lavish use of depth, and an elegant play of light and shade mark his mature hand.
britannica-1911-motril:
Motril, a town of southern Spain in the province of Granada, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands at the foot of a spur of the Sierra Nevada, on the edge of a rich plain of river soil. The sea lies about one mile away. Granada sits forty miles to the north north east, joined by a good carriage road.

The count in 1900 was 18528 people, and the climate is half tropical in kind. That plain has proved fit in a high degree for sugar cane and sugar beet. Sugar factories crowd the district, most of all at Salobreña three miles west. Cotton is grown and made up there as well. Other goods span alcohol, flour, soap, iron wares, and cotton cloth. Zinc and lead enrich the ground round the town. Grapes, figs, almonds, and zinc go out as exports.
britannica-1911-nail:
Nail names two quite unlike things, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica covers both senses. One is the horny cover on fingers and toes in humans and apes. The other is a headed spike of metal, most often iron. That second sense fills most of the entry by far.

Metal nails sort by size, head shape, point, and method of making. Hand wrought, machine cut, wire, and cast forms are the four main classes. Hand nail making around Birmingham once employed whole families in poor sheds. Machines later took over most of that trade. Horse nails alone still called for hand work in fine iron.
britannica-1911-natal-brazil:
Natal is a city article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Natal is a city and port of Brazil, capital of the state of Rio Grande do Norte. It stands on the right bank of the Rio Potengy, near the river's mouth. Coastwise steamers call there, anchoring outside the bar.

The entry gives a blunt picture of the place. It calls Natal a stagnant, poorly built town of one-storey houses and mud-walled cabins. Few public buildings rose above that level. Cotton making was the only industry of note, and exports were chiefly sugar and cotton. A short history follows: the town was founded in 1597 as a military post. The Dutch held it from 1633 to 1654. It became a provincial capital in 1820. Early works sometimes called it the City of the Kings.
britannica-1911-order-in-council:
Order in Council is the subject of a government article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In Great Britain an order in council is an order issued by the sovereign on the advice of the privy council. More often it rests on the advice of a few chosen members. It is the modern form of the old royal ordinance. Unlike a statute, it does not need the assent of parliament.

The article notes that such orders rest in theory on royal power alone. In practice they issue only on the advice of ministers, who answer to parliament for them. Fear that orders might change the law has led parliament to pass acts shielding those who issued them. The most famed use came in 1807, in war with France. Orders then barred all ships, on pain of seizure, from trading with ports under French sway.
britannica-1911-pail: Pail, a bucket for carrying water, milk or other liquids, is given a short word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Such vessels are made of wood, metal or other stuff, round in form and most often wider at the top than at the base. The entry says the root of the word is not clear. One path points to an old English word for a small wine measure, the other to an old French word for a small pan, and neither fits a deep vessel well.
britannica-1911-poppy-oil:
Oil pressed from poppy seed is laid out in a trade entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Both white seed and black seed of the poppy serve the press. Black seed is the pick when oil is the main crop aim. Seeds hold from fifty to sixty parts oil in the hundred. A cold first press gives the fine white grade of oil.

That first oil runs clear, pale, bland, and near scent free. A hot second press adds a coarser, redder grade with bite. The oil dries fast, faster than raw linseed oil in fact. Painters prize it as a medium for oil work on canvas. North France and Germany use the fine grades as salad oil. Poor grades go to soap, varnish, and lamps.
britannica-1911-privy-council:
Privy Council is the subject of a government article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its origin goes back in substance to the Norman period of English history. The great assembly of crown tenants held within it a smaller group of state and household officers. With clerks and secretaries, that group ran the business of government. Their duties were to advise the king, see justice done, and carry out his will.

The article explains how such blended power could last only while affairs stayed simple. As government grew more settled and complex, a split of powers followed. Finance broke away first, into a separate office at the exchequer. Courts of law then grew into being as bodies of their own. Yet the king stayed the fountain of justice for cases the ordinary courts could not reach. Relieved of money detail and most court work, the council kept growing.
britannica-1911-quail:
The quail is the subject of a bird entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives its names in French, Italian, Dutch, German, and Danish at the start. The bird was well known across most of Europe, Asia, and Africa. Its Latin name is given as Coturnix communis.

Inside, the text notes the odd three part call of the male bird. That call was copied in rough form in several tongues. In parts of Britain the bird was known by nicknames tied to that call. Its plumage is described as reddish brown above. Each feather bears dark marks crossed by a pale stripe down its length.
britannica-1911-retail: Retail means the sale of goods in small amounts to the person who will use them, as the short 1911 Britannica entry explains. It stands against wholesale, the sale of goods in bulk. The word comes from an old French term for a piece cut off. Kindred English words from the same Latin root for a cutting include entail, tailor, detail, and tally. A second sense of the verb, to tell a tale again, grew from an old sense of selling at second hand.
britannica-1911-robert-the-devil:
Robert the Devil is the hero of a romance, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells his strange tale in full. He was the son of a duke of Normandy, and by twenty a marvel of strength. He used that strength only for outrage and crime. At last his mother told him the cause of his wicked urges: he had been born in answer to prayers made to the devil.

The pope sent him to a hermit, who laid a hard penance on him. He must keep utter silence, feign madness, take his food from a dog's mouth, and bear abuse from the crowd without striking back. He became court fool to the emperor at Rome. Three years running he saved the city from Saracen attack as an unknown knight. Offered the emperor's daughter, he refused and ended his days in a hermitage.
britannica-1911-rottweil:
Rottweil is a town in Wurttemberg in Germany, described in a 1911 Britannica town entry. It stands on a hill on the left bank of the Neckar river. The town held just over nine thousand people in 1905 and keeps part of its old walls. Two fine Gothic churches anchor its sights, one with a spire two hundred and thirty feet high.

A chapel in town holds old German carvings and pictures of note, plus a Roman mosaic. Local work spans powder, locomotives, machines, cotton, leather, and beer. In the 1200s the town became a free imperial city with a famed court. That court judged cases across Swabia, the Rhineland, and Alsace until 1784.
britannica-1911-spandril: Spandril, or spandrel, is a term of building defined in a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word is of unknown origin. It names the space between any arch or curved brace and the level beam above it. The spandrils over doorways in the Perpendicular style are most often richly dressed with carving. At Magdalen College in Oxford one such space is pierced through, with a most lovely effect. The space seldom forms part of the design of the doorway itself.
britannica-1911-stencil:
Stencil names a thin plate cut with a pattern, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The plate may be metal, leather, paper, or another thin stuff. It is laid upon a surface that is to be marked. Colour or ink is then brushed or rubbed across it. The design cut out is left printed on the ground beneath.

In pottery work the stencil plays a different part. There a coating guards parts of the ware from the printed pattern or enamel. The guarded parts keep the biscuit's own colour in the finished piece. The word is traced to an earlier form, stinsel, by the scholar Skeat. Behind that stands a French verb meaning to sparkle, or powder with stars. Its root is the Latin word for a spark. The same French word gave English its tinsel, the glittering stuff used to dress up cloth.
britannica-1911-tourneur-cyril:
Cyril Tourneur (about 1575-1626) was an English dramatist, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica pieces together his sparse record. He may have been the son of a captain who served in the Netherlands, and Tourneur himself served in the Low Countries. In 1613 he was paid for carrying letters to Brussels.

The entry notes his government pension and his post as secretary to a council of war in 1625, before he sailed to Cadiz with Sir Edward Cecil. He died in Ireland on the way home. His fame rests on two plays, published in 1607 and 1611, though the entry argues the later printed one was written first.
britannica-1911-trinidad-brazil: Trinidad is a bare island in the South Atlantic, east of the coast of Espirito Santo in Brazil. It is four miles long by two miles broad and was formed by volcanoes. It has springs of fresh water but no people live there. As a site for coal and cables in mid ocean, it caused a dispute in eighteen ninety five. Brazil and Great Britain both claimed the island that year. The case was settled in favour of Brazil. Three small islets called Martin Vaz lie about thirty miles east.
britannica-1911-veil:
A veil is a cloth used to hide something from view. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces the word to the Latin velum, a sail or cloth. Veils hung before the holy places in the Jewish tabernacle. The word is used most, though, of a cover for a woman's face and head. In lands shaped by Islam, women veil when out of the house. Slaves, the very poor, and Bedouin women are largely exempt.

Forms of the veil fill the middle of the entry. The burka is a long strip of white muslin over the whole face. The poor wear it in coarse black cloth instead. In Europe the veil long formed part of women's dress. In modern use it is gauze or lace fixed to a hat. It guards the face from dust, light, and wind.
britannica-1911-whale-oil:
Whale-oil is an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica that traces the whale fisheries and the oils they yielded. The text opens in the far north, where the fall fishing went on near Point Barrow between seasons of sperm whaling in the south. The Bering Strait fishery began in 1848, and in the three years after, 250 ships took cargoes there. In 1871 no fewer than 34 ships were left in the ice off Cape Belcher.

The sperm whale fishery yields spermaceti, sperm oil, ambergris, and teeth. Americans began it in 1690, and the British opened the great grounds of the Pacific and Indian Oceans, reaching a peak in 1791 with 75 ships from London alone. By 1853 sperm whaling had ceased as a British trade. The American fleet stood at 735 ships in 1846 but sank to an average of 159 in the decade after 1877.
britannica-1911-yggdrasil:
Yggdrasil, in the myths of Scandinavia, is the great ash tree that stands for all being. The 1911 Britannica article says it binds earth, heaven, and hell in one frame. It is the tree of life, of wisdom, of fate, of time, and of space. Its stem holds up the earth. Its boughs shade the world and reach past the sky. Three roots run down into three great realms below.

One root sinks to the realm of death, where the dragon Nidhug gnaws it in a well. One runs to the realm of the giants, where the spring of Mimer holds the source of wisdom. One runs to Asgard, home of the gods, where the Fates dwell by a sacred spring. An eagle sits on the top bough. A squirrel runs up and down to stir strife between eagle and dragon. On this tree Odin hung for nine nights.
catalogue-of-violent-and-destructive-ear:
Rev. Miguel Saderra Masó, assistant director of the Weather Bureau in Manila, compiled his catalogue of Philippine earthquakes for the general list that John Milne was preparing for the British Association. Printed at Manila in 1910, it covers the years 1599 to 1909 and takes in only shocks strong enough to crack buildings or worse.

Each entry gives the date, the hour, an intensity on the Rossi-Forel scale, and the places hit, with short notes on damage. A destructive shock at Surigao in 1879, rated ten, left no stone building fit to live in. An appendix extends the same treatment to the Marianas Islands. Observatory science and colonial records meet in the tables.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-luxe:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Luxeuil describes a monastery in Franche-Comté, the great Irish monk Columbanus founded it in 585 on Luxovium's ruined Roman castle. Named for St. Peter, it soon became Gaul's most famed and great monastery.

The monks were so many that choir followed choir in chanting the Office, and here first sounded the laus perennis, the endless chant day and night. Columbanus' rule, borrowed mostly from Irish houses, did not long prevail, and the entry weighs his forceful, fiery nature against St. Benedict's care. Luxeuil's sway, its rule and its founder's nature form the entry's centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albero-de-mon:
Albero de Montreuil was Archbishop of Trier, born near Toul in Lorraine about 1080 and dead at Coblenz in 1152. After holding posts in the churches of Toul and Verdun, he became Archdeacon and Provost of St. Arnulf at Metz. There he joined the church reform party against Bishop Adalbero IV and travelled to Rome in person to seek the bishop's removal by Pope Paschal II.

Back home, Albero helped secure Theotger's election: the Black Forest abbot of St. George took office unwillingly in July 1118. As archbishop he pressed reform with vigour and restored peace and order in his archdiocese. The entry draws on the metrical Deeds of Albero and other medieval histories of Trier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-rail:
The altar rail guards the sanctuary, separating it from the church's body, and is also called the communion rail, since the faithful kneel there for Holy Communion. Carved wood, metal, marble, or other precious material forms it. It stands about two feet six inches high and six to nine inches wide on top.

A clean white linen cloth, about two feet wide and the rail's full length, spreads before communicants to catch particles falling from the priest's hands. Each communicant holds it under the chin in both hands. Lace or netting would defeat its purpose, though a fine lace or embroidered border is allowed. A gilt paten, salver, or larger pall may replace the cloth, passed along the rail, never a consecrated paten in lay hands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-gaubi:
Antoine Gaubil, a French Jesuit missionary born in 1689, spent nearly forty years at Peking as astronomer and historian. He reached China in 1722 and stayed until his death, heading a school where Manchus learned Latin for Russian affairs. His Chinese name was Sun Kiun-yung, and his letters reached scholars across Europe.

From Chinese sources he translated a history of Genghis Khan and part of the Tang annals, and he wrote a treatise on Chinese chronology. His study of Chinese astronomy appeared in a Paris collection, and his version of the Book of History followed after his death. The entry calls him the best astronomer and historian among French Jesuits in China of his century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-margi:
Valencia-born Franciscan Antonio Margil, who lived from 1657 to 1726, volunteered for the Indian missions of America after joining his order in 1673 and reaching Vera Cruz in 1683. Stationed at the missionary college of Santa Cruz, Querétaro, he worked across Mexico, Yucatán, Costa Rica, and Nicaragua. Above all he worked in Guatemala, where he earned the name Apostle of Guatemala. He walked barefoot, fasted every day, ate neither meat nor fish, and spent most of the night in prayer.

In 1706 he became first guardian, or head, of the new missionary college of Guadalupe at Zacatecas. Ten years later he led three priests and two lay brothers into Texas, founding missions of Guadalupe among the Nacogdoches, Dolores for the Ays, and San Miguel among other peoples. The article credits his harsh penance and tireless travel with extraordinary success among Indians and colonists alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardo-buil:
Bernardo Buil, also spelled Boil or Boyl, a Franciscan friar, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Confusion clouds him because two Spaniards of the name lived at once, one Franciscan and one Benedictine, and some writers merged them into a single man. The entry argues they were distinct.

To the Franciscan, Pope Alexander VI addressed a bull of June 1493 appointing him the pope's first deputy for the New World, the pope's deputy for the newly found lands. He sailed with Columbus's second voyage and quarrelled with the admiral over treatment of the natives. The piece untangles an identity puzzle at the dawn of American missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brazil:
Brazil, a republic larger than the United States without Alaska and the Philippines, spans 3,218,130 square miles from 5 degrees north to 33 degrees south. It borders every South American country except Chile, with the Amazon basin's low Selvas in the north and west and plateaus of 2,000 to 4,000 feet in the south and east. Its Atlantic coast runs about 4,000 miles, and its rivers rank among the world's greatest travel routes.

Mountain systems include the Serra do Mar, rising to Itatiaia near 10,000 feet, the Serra Central, and a northwestern range dividing the Sao Francisco and Tocantins from the Parana. Later sections cover climate, farming, minerals, manufactures, railroads, commerce, population, government, religion, church organization, schools, and history, giving a full portrait of the young republic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devil:
A doctrinal entry on the devil, the name commonly given to fallen angels, also called demons. With the definite article it means Lucifer, their chief, as in Matthew's phrase about the devil and his angels. Greek diabolos means slanderer or accuser, matching the Hebrew Satan, an adversary, and the name marks an office, not a nature.

No single passage gives the full teaching: scattered notices from Genesis to Apocalypse must be read together with patristic tradition. The Fourth Lateran Council states the Church line, that devil and demons were created good by God and made themselves evil. Later pages follow the scriptural trail and close with Paul's armour passage, urging truth, justice, peace, and the shield of faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dicuil:
Dicuil was an Irish monk and geographer of the late eighth century. He worked in a monastery of the Frankish kingdom and knew the islands near England and Scotland from his own travel. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows his two surviving works. One is an astronomical computus written between 814 and 816, and the other is a geography finished in 825.

His geography, On the Measurement of the World, drew on a survey ordered by the emperor Theodosius the Second. It also drew on Pliny and Isidore of Seville, while adding what Dicuil had seen himself. The entry gives a clear portrait of a monk who joined book learning to firsthand knowledge of distant shores.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eskil:
Eskil was Archbishop of Lund in Skåne, Sweden, born about 1100 and dead at Clairvaux on 6 September 1181. He was one of Scandinavia's most capable princes of the Church. A man of profound piety, he defended the hierarchy courageously against civil power and clerical usurpers. His father Christian descended from an illustrious Jutland family related to several royal houses.

At twelve Eskil entered the cathedral school at Hildesheim. During a dangerous illness he saw a vision of the Mother of God, who chided his frivolous conduct, saved him, and demanded five measures of corn as a thank-offering. The vision was read to mean he would rise high and establish five confraternities. In 1131 his uncle Asser, first Archbishop of Lund, made him provost of the cathedral. In 1134 he became Bishop of Roskilde, and after Asser's death in 1137 succeeded him as archbishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-de-ca:
Etienne de Carheil, a French missionary among the Indians of Canada, was born at Carentoir in France in November 1633 and died at Quebec on 27 July 1726. He joined the Society of Jesus at Paris in 1652, studied at Amiens, La Flèche, and Bourges, and taught at Rouen and Tours. Ordained in 1666, he sailed for Canada and spent two years at Quebec preparing for mission work.

He had longed to die for Christ. Instead, thirty years of hardship among the Hurons and Iroquois became his martyrdom in Canada. Cayuga was his first mission, until the chiefs drove him out in 1684. Three years teaching grammar at the College of Quebec followed, and then came his assignment to the Mission of Mackinac. His opposition to the brandy traffic angered La Mothe Cadillac, commandant at Mackinac, and he was compelled to return to Quebec in 1703.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-evil:
Evil, in the large sense used here, is the sum of all that stands against human desires and needs, and hence of the suffering that fills life. The entry first defines its kinds. Physical evil covers sickness, accident, death, poverty, and oppression, and all that thwarts man's powers by nature or by faulty social order. Moral evil is the will turning from the moral order toward ends conscience condemns. Metaphysical evil is the mutual limit of natural things, by which none reaches full perfection, as beasts prey on beasts and storms wreck the order of nature.

The article then argues that all evil is at root negative, a loss or lack of some good needful for perfection, not a thing in itself. Wrong action adds a positive choice, yet its evil lies in turning from right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fifth-lateran:
The Fifth Lateran Council met at Rome from 1512 to 1517. Pope Julius II called it to answer the rebel cardinals' council at Pisa. Fifteen cardinals, ten archbishops, and fifty-six bishops attended its opening. Leo X continued it to its twelfth session after Julius died in February 1513.

The council finally revoked the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges in 1516. It approved a new concordat with Francis I of France. It sanctioned montes pietatis, pawn shops for the necessitous poor under strict church control. It also banned printing books without the permission of the diocesan bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-lateran:
The First Lateran Council met at Rome in March 1123, under Callistus II in person. It followed the Concordat of Worms of 1122, the first agreement of its kind between pope and emperor. More than three hundred bishops and six hundred abbots assembled for the council. Both originals of the Concordat were read aloud and ratified by the assembly.

The council issued twenty-two disciplinary canons, mostly restating earlier decrees. Clerical marriage was forbidden, and marriages of clerics were declared null by law. Crusaders' families and goods gained safeguards, and lay seizure of church offerings drew excommunication. Abbots were barred from penance, sick visits, and extreme unction, and took their holy oils from their bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fourth-latera:
The Fourth Lateran Council met at Rome in November 1215, summoned by Pope Innocent III, who had planned a general council from the start of his reign. It was huge: seventy-one patriarchs and metropolitans, 412 bishops, and 900 abbots and priors. Envoys came from Emperor Frederick II and the kings of France, England, Aragon, Hungary, Cyprus, and Jerusalem.

The fathers did little more than approve seventy decrees Innocent had already drawn up, but that approval gave them ecumenical force. Canon 1 set out the Catholic faith and the doctrine of transubstantiation, the change of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ. Other canons condemned heretics, set yearly provincial councils, barred new religious orders, and curbed clerical abuses. In the famous Canon 21, every Christian of age to confess and receive communion at least once a year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giraud-de-bor:
Giraud de Borneil was a Provençal troubadour born at Excideuil in the viscounty of Limoges around the middle of the twelfth century. His exact dates are unknown, but the best authorities place his life between 1160 and 1219. Of humble birth, he counted kings among his patrons, including Richard the Lionheart, whom he followed to Palestine on the Third Crusade. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the master of the troubadours.

In winter he studied literature in the schools, and in summer, with two singers reciting his songs, he toured the courts of his royal patrons. Unmarried, he left his property at death to poor relations and his parish church of Saint-Gervais. About eighty poems survive with some certainty, scattered through collections. His early verse in the obscure trobar clus gave way to the easy, simple poetry he praised in his tensons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guayaquil:
Ecuador's port of Guayaquil, on the lower Guayas river, was founded by Benalcázar in 1535 and grew into the country's second city after Quito. Fear of earthquakes made it a city built almost wholly of wood, even its double-towered cathedral, so fire destroyed it again and again, most recently in 1896 and 1902.

Its bishopric, set up in February 1837 from Cuenca, first answered to Lima and then to Quito from 1849. It covers 11,500 square miles with 130,900 souls, 40 parishes, and a seminary and colleges. Bishops Garaycoa, Aguirre, and the Jesuits Lizarzabaru and del Pozo lead a roll that runs beside shipping figures, a Salesian school of 600 scholars, and a Dominican convent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-humeral-veil:
The humeral veil is a rectangular cloth about eight feet long and one and a half feet wide. It is worn over the back and shoulders, hence its name, with its ends hanging down in front. The Roman Ceremonial requires silk, edges are usually fringed, and a cross with the name Jesus or some other device adorns the centre. Festival veils are often richly embroidered.

Pockets or flaps under the lower edges let the wearer hold objects without wearing the veil itself out too fast. Clasps or ribbons across the breast keep it from slipping. The veil serves at solemn high Mass, where the subdeacon holds the paten in it from the Offertory to after the Pater Noster. It serves at pontifical Mass for the bishop's mitre, and in processions and benedictions where the sacred vessel must be carried veiled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hyacinthe-sig:
Hyacinthe-Sigismond Gerdil was a Savoyard cardinal and theologian, born at Samoëns in 1718 and dead at Rome in 1802. At fifteen he joined the Barnabites at Annecy and studied theology at Bologna, where Archbishop Lambertini, later Benedict XIV, noticed his success across many branches of knowledge. He taught philosophy at Macerata and at Turin, became provincial of his order, and tutored the Prince of Piedmont.

Named cardinal in petto in 1773 by Clement XIV, Gerdil was promoted by Pius VI in 1777. Pius named him Dibbon's bishop, Holy Office consultor, corrector of oriental books, and Propaganda prefect. After Rome's invasion in 1798 he retired to his Abbey of Della Chiusa. At Venice in 1800 he would probably have been elected pope had Cardinal Herzan not vetoed him for the German emperor, and he then accompanied Pius VII to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-de-montm:
John de Montmirail was a French nobleman who gave up court life and wealth for Cistercian poverty. Born in 1165 to the Lord of Montmirail, His mother trained him in piety. He embraced a military career and formed a lasting friendship with Philip Augustus at the royal court. Court dissipations dulled his early training, and even marriage to the estimable Helvide de Dampierre did not reform him.

In his thirtieth year the counsel of Jobert, prior of St. Etienne, converted him. He turned to God with generosity, building a hospital for the sick with special care for lepers. He loved the poor as brothers, wore a hair shirt, and spent whole nights in prayer. After trying the life of a recluse, he entered the Cistercian monastery of Longpont, giving his goods to the poor. He died in 1217, with miracles reported at his tomb ever since.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-kreil:
Karl Kreil was an Austrian meteorologist and astronomer, born at Ried in Upper Austria in 1798 and dead at Vienna in 1862. Schooled at Kremsmünster Abbey under Boniface Schwarzenbrunner, he joined its observatory work. He studied law for financial reasons, but abandoned it in 1823 for mathematics and physics. He served at Vienna in 1827, at Milan's Brera in 1831, and as director of Prague's observatory from 1845.

Finding Prague's observatory in poor condition, he turned to terrestrial observation and introduced terrestrial physics into Austria. Through personal privation he built a system of magnetic and meteorological observation rivaling Göttingen under Gauss. His plan for a central Austrian station was realized at Vienna in 1851, with Kreil as first director and professor of physics. His observations spread from Bohemia over the empire to the Adriatic, Turkey, and the Black Sea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgy-of-st:
The Liturgy of St. Basil gathers the Eastern rites linked to Basil, Bishop of Caesarea from 370 to 379. That Basil reshaped an older liturgy is firm, backed by Byzantine tradition and by many old witnesses, though several distinct forms now bear his name.

Proclus reports that Basil cut a long rite short when worshippers flagged, and Peter the Deacon quoted a Basil prayer in a letter around 520. Leontius praised Basil's rite against Theodore's new Mass, and the Trullan Council of 692 cited his written liturgy. The entry sorts the surviving Greek, Syriac, and other forms that claim his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-pierre-:
Louis Pierre Anquetil was a French historian, born at Paris in 1723 and dead in 1806. He joined the Congregation of Sainte-Geneviève at seventeen, taught theology and letters, directed the Reims seminary, and wrote a history of that city.

Prior at La Roee, director at Senlis, and holder of a priory at Chateau-Renard, he wrote a history of the League, then of the Fronde troubles. Jailed at Saint Lazare during the Terror, he worked there on his Universal History, finished after Thermidor. His History of France, done at Napoleon's request, shows old age's weakening grip, and Thierry judged it cold and colourless beside Mezeray and Daniel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montreuil:
Montreuil is the Charterhouse of Notre-Dame-des-Pres in the Diocese of Arras, Pas-de-Calais. Its founder was Robert, Count of Boulogne and Auvergne. The charter bears the date 15 July 1324 from Hardelot castle, and the church was consecrated in 1338. Lying near Calais, it suffered repeated sackings by the English in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. At times it was abandoned.

Imperial troops wrecked it again in 1542. The wars of religion brought fresh troubles. Dom Bernard Bruyant rebuilt it late in the seventeenth century, leaving it quiet until the Revolution suppressed it in 1790 and sold its property. Eighty-two years later the Carthusians bought back part of the estate. They laid a new foundation stone in 1872 and finished in three years, with twenty-four cells and a noted press for order publications.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-odo-of-glanfe:
Odo of Glanfeuil, ninth-century abbot and hagiographer, gave Saint Maurus a French legend that scholars still doubt. Entering Glanfeuil by 856 and abbot by 861, he issued a Life of Maurus in 864, claiming to revise a life by Faustus of Montecassino that makes Maurus founder of Glanfeuil.

Its anachronisms persuade most critics that Odo wrote it himself, though Mabillon defended Faustus. Odo's Miracles of Saint Maurus, with more solid history, tells how he fled Normans with the relics in 862 and moved them to Saint-Maur-des-Fossés in 868. Mabillon and a few modern writers still ascribe the Life to Faustus, against the majority view.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulus-bril:
Paulus Bril was a gifted Flemish painter and engraver born at Antwerp in 1556 and dead at Rome on 7 October 1626. He first studied with Damiaen Oertelmans. News of his brother Matthys's success at Rome drew him from his parents to that city. Held at Lyons for lack of funds, he worked to fund the journey onward.

At Rome he studied with his brother, but drew best inspiration later from copying Titian's landscapes. On that basis he built a vigorous style, said to have greatly advanced landscape art through influence on Rubens, Carracci, and Claude Lorraine. He aided his brother's Vatican works, and on Matthys's death in 1584 continued their joint labour for Gregory XIII. His chief Vatican work is a sixty-eight-foot fresco for the Sala Clementina, ordered by Clement VIII, showing Saint Clement cast into the sea with an anchor at his neck.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippe-avri:
Philippe Avril was a French Jesuit traveller, born at Angoulême in 1654. Professor of philosophy and mathematics at Paris, he was summoned to the China missions and, following Father Verbiest's instructions from Peking, attempted the overland route. Six years of travel carried him through Kurdistan, Armenia, Astrakhan, Persia, and other eastern lands.

At Moscow he was refused passage through Tatary and sent by the government to Poland, from which he made his way to Constantinople and back to France. Worn out by haemorrhages, he nevertheless embarked again on a vessel that was lost at sea, and he died in the shipwreck of 1698. His accounts of his long wanderings remain interesting and valuable records of lands then little known to Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plenary-counc:
A plenary council is a church synod that represents the whole body of bishops of a given territory. The Latin plenarium means complete or full, and Saint Augustine already called ecumenical councils plenary, since they represent the entire Church. Provincial councils earned the name because every bishop of the province attended.

Later usage narrowed the term to councils called by a delegate of the Apostolic See with special powers. Those councils were attended by all metropolitans and bishops of a kingdom or commonwealth or their representatives. Such synods are often called national councils, and the entry traces them from third-century gatherings at Iconium and Synnada through the plenary councils of all Africa under the Archbishop of Carthage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polydore-verg:
Polydore Vergil was an Italian-born historian of England and a pioneer of modern historical method. He was born at Urbino about 1470, studied at Bologna and Padua, and served the Duke of Urbino and Alexander VI. His early works, a book of proverbs and On the Inventors of Things, won extraordinary popularity.

Sent to England in 1501 as sub-collector of Peter's Pence, he became intimate with Henry VII, who in 1505 commissioned his History of England. Published in 1533 and prized above all for Henry VII's reign, it consulted authorities, weighed evidence, and told a connected story rather than a bare chronicle. Offending Wolsey cost him prison and his collectorship, and he avenged himself with a hostile portrait of Wolsey in the history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-provincial-co:
A provincial council is a deliberative assembly of the bishops of a church province. The metropolitan archbishop calls it and chairs it, to debate common business and set disciplinary rules. This encyclopedia entry shows why such groupings arose. A church as vast as the Catholic Church needed dioceses with shared interests to act together while general canon law was still taking shape. Early councils ordered bishops to meet twice a year, at Nicaea in 325 and Antioch in 341.

Attendance was a strict duty for bishops. Those who stayed away without good excuse faced censure. In early times slack bishops lost communion with their fellows. Others joined for counsel without a vote. They included non-exempt abbots, deputies of cathedral chapters, heads of religious orders, university deputies, seminary rectors, and the council's theologians and canonists. The entry closes by pointing to the great collections where decrees from Trent to 1870 are printed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-vei:
In ancient Rome a red veil, or one with red stripes, marked newly married women apart from the unmarried. From the earliest times Christ was set before the Christian virgin as a husband, the only one, in Saint Paul's words, she had to please. As the vestal virgins had done, the bride of Christ naturally took the veil, which symbolized less purity than inviolable fidelity to Christ, a fidelity to be reverenced in her. Saint Optatus called the bond a sort of spiritual marriage.

Taking the veil thus suggested an obligation of constancy: first it forbade illicit intercourse, and afterwards marriage itself. Virgins took the veil themselves or received it from their parents' hands. Widows who professed continence wore it too, and the entry follows the veil from Roman marriage custom into the consecration of virgins in the Roman Pontifical.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-goupil:
René Goupil, Jesuit missionary, was born in Anjou in 1607 and martyred in New York State on 23 September 1642. Poor health kept him from joining the Society regularly, so he volunteered to serve it without pay in Canada as a donné. After two years as a surgeon in the Quebec hospitals, he set out in 1642 for the Huron mission with Father Jogues, remaining his constant companion and disciple until death.

Captured by the Iroquois near Lake Saint Peter, he accepted his fate without resistance. He shared the other captives' beating: nails torn out, finger joints cut off. The thirteen days' march to Iroquois country brought heat, hunger, blows, and festering wounds. Forced to march between double ranks of two hundred warriors, he was almost beaten to death, yet when he might have escaped, he stayed with Jogues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-lalor:
Richard Lalor Sheil was an Irish dramatist, writer, and politician whose voice helped carry the campaign for Catholic Emancipation. Born in County Kilkenny in 1791, he was schooled at home, at Kensington, and at Stonyhurst, then entered Trinity College Dublin and qualified at the Irish Bar in 1814. When family money failed, he turned to the stage, and plays such as Adelaide, The Apostate, and Evadne brought him both fame and income.

Politics soon claimed more of his energy. At first he favoured gentle petitioning and compromise with Protestant opinion, but he came round to Daniel O'Connell's bolder agitation, demanding emancipation as a right rather than a favour. In the Catholic Association he stood second only to O'Connell, and his Sketches of the Irish Bar preserved vivid portraits of the lawyers and leaders of his day. He died at Florence in 1851.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-nanteu:
Robert Nanteuil was a French engraver and crayon portraitist who raised engraving to fine art. Born at Reims in 1623, a merchant's son, he was sent to a Jesuit school that gave him learning but no encouragement to draw. In spare moments he worked with pencil and burin. Benedictines later fostered his gift; one monk sat for his Buste d'un Religieux of 1644.

In financial straits, he went to Paris in 1648 and worked with Regnesson, whose sister he married. His method moved from straight lines alone to cross-hatching and stippling for middle tones. Crayon portraits won him a pension and the post of Royal Engraver in 1658, with a Gobelins studio. In 1660 Louis XIV, largely at his prompting, issued an edict giving engravers the privileges of other artists. He made nineteen portraits of the king alone and wrote verses often printed beneath his portraits. He died at Paris in 1678.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rule-of-st-ba:
Under the name Basilians fall all religious who follow the Rule of St Basil. Their monasteries never had the organization of a proper order's houses. Basil drew up his Rule for the monastery he founded about 356 on the Iris in Cappadocia, after visiting Egypt, Palestine, and Mesopotamia. Gregory of Nazianzus, who shared the retreat, aided him with advice and experience.

The Rule divides into Greater Monastic Rules and Lesser Rules. Rufinus, translating them into Latin, joined both into a single Rule followed by some western monasteries. Basil's method is catechetical: the disciple poses a question, the master answers. He lays down indisputable principles to guide superiors and monks, sending them to Scripture as the true Rule. Questions concern virtues to practise and vices to avoid. Its striking qualities are prudence and wisdom: superiors settle daily details, while poverty, obedience, renunciation, and self-abnegation ground monastic life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-maria-b:
Santa Maria, a Brazilian see suffragan of Porto Alegre, was one of three new sees cut from São Pedro do Rio Grande do Sul. Pius X raised that see to an archdiocese on 15 August 1910. Pelotas and Uruguayana were the other two. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sketches a young diocese of farming colonies.

Santa Maria holds twenty-two parishes across the central and northern parts of Rio Grande do Sul, a mild, wooded, fertile country where German and Italian colonists farm and raise cattle. Nearly everyone is Catholic. Cachoeira on the Jacuhy river, 120 miles west of Porto Alegre by steamboat and rail, ranks as chief town, with Rio Pardo, Santa Maria, Passo Fundo, and Cruz Alta behind it. Lima de Valverde became first bishop in 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sao-paulo-bra:
São Paulo, an ecclesiastical province in Brazil, gathers the dioceses of Campinas, Ribeirão Preto, Taubaté, Botucatú, Corityba, and São Carlos do Pinhal, all in São Paulo state. Made a bishopric in 1745, it rose to metropolitan rank in 1908, when those dioceses were created with it. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia gives the province's strength in figures.

Over 2,500,000 Catholics lived in the province in 1910, served by 203 secular and fifty regular priests across seven orders, with four convents, 530 churches and chapels, and thirty-six Catholic schools. In the city of São Paulo stand the provincial and central seminaries and a girls' seminary under the Sisters of St Joseph. Benedictine and Marist colleges and the Lyceu of Our Lady of Mount Carmel complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-second-latera:
The Second Lateran Council, tenth ecumenical council, was convoked by Innocent II in April 1139 after a schism that followed Honorius II's death in February 1130. Petrus Leonis, as Anacletus II, long checked the lawful pope, backed by Bernard and Norbert, until Anacletus died in January 1138. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a council meant to erase a schism's traces.

Innocent had held a council at Pisa in 1135 and gained ground steadily. At the Lateran nearly a thousand prelates from most Christian nations gathered. The pope opened with a discourse and deposed those ordained or instituted by the antipope and his chief backers, Aegidius of Tusculum and Gerard of Angoulême.
