Roger of Sicily, Anacletus's partisan reconciled with Innocent, still upheld schism in southern Italy, and the council condemned errors and reformed clerical and popular abuses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-boisil:
St. Boisil was superior of Melrose Abbey, dead in 664, and this entry follows a man known almost entirely from Bede. Almost all we know of Boisil comes from Bede's Ecclesiastical History and Life of Cuthbert. Bede learned it from Sigfrid, a monk of Jarrow previously trained by Boisil at Melrose. Boisil's fame rests mainly on his great pupil, St. Cuthbert, but the master was plainly worthy of the disciple.

Boisil's supernatural intuitions deeply impressed his contemporaries. When Cuthbert arrived at Melrose, Boisil exclaimed, Behold a servant of the Lord, and got Abbot Eata's leave to receive him into the community at once. When Cuthbert fell sick in the great pestilence of 664, Boisil declared his certain recovery. Somewhat later Boisil himself, as foretold three years before, fell victim to that epidemic, but before the end he predicted Cuthbert would become a bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-holy-grai:
A legendary sacred vessel, sometimes the chalice of the Eucharist and sometimes the dish of the Paschal lamb, anchors this entry on medieval romance. In the romances its nature shifts and often stays vague; Chrétien's Perceval leaves it wholly unexplained. Its name too has drawn many guesses, and the entry sifts them with care.

Helinandus, a Cistercian chronicler who died about 1230, supplies the accepted account. Under the year 717 he tells of a hermit's vision of the dish used at the Last Supper, written up as the Gradale. French gradalis meant a wide, deep dish serving costly foods in courses, while popular speech called it greal, pleasant to the eater. Romance cycles built a quest upon it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-third-lateran:
Lateran Council of 1179, third of that name, closes this slice with Alexander III's laborious pontificate. Like 1139, its task was to repair evils from an antipope's schism. Back in Rome on 12 March 1178, Alexander took citizens' oaths of fidelity and needful guarantees. He then welcomed antipope Callistus III, John de Struma, who yielded at Tusculum on 29 August 1178 after Christian of Mainz besieged him at Viterbo.

Alexander received Callistus with kindness and made him Governor of Beneventum. Obstinate partisans picked Lando Sitino as a new antipope Innocent III, but lacking support he soon gave up and retired to La Cava monastery. In September 1178, under the Peace of Venice, the pope called an ecumenical council at the Lateran for the next Lent, sending legates far and wide. Its canons on elections and discipline shaped the medieval Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vatican-counc:
The Vatican Council, the twentieth ecumenical council and, to 1912, the last, opened on 8 December 1869 and adjourned on 20 October 1870, three hundred years after Trent. Its earlier history begins on 6 December 1864, two days before the Syllabus appeared, when Pius IX told the Congregation of Rites of his plan to summon a general council. He asked Rome's cardinals to write their views on the plan's wisdom and on subjects for discussion.

Of twenty-one reports sent in, only Cardinal Pentini's held that no council was needed; the rest backed the scheme. The entry follows the preparations, the council's sessions, its debates on faith and on papal infallibility, and its abrupt adjournment when Italian troops entered Rome. It closes with the council's constitutions and their reception, a full history of a council cut short by war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vaudreuil:
Philippe de Rigaud, Marquis de Vaudreuil, governed Canada as its governor, born in Languedoc in the first half of the seventeenth century to Louis de Vaudreuil and Marie de Château-Verdun. He died at Quebec on 10 October 1725. In the king's musketeers, where he served from 1659 to 1676, he rose to brigadier and finally colonel. He reached Canada in 1687 commanding a marine detachment.

After the Lachine massacre he kept the Iroquois from attacking Montreal in 1689, and in 1690 he shared in Quebec's defence against Phips. In 1698 he won the Cross of St Louis and succeeded Callières as Governor of Montreal. In 1702 he received the fief still bearing his name, and in 1703 he again succeeded Callières, now as governor-general, guiding the colony through a trying age.
compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers-o:
Compilation of the Messages and Papers of the Presidents: William McKinley gathers the state papers of McKinley's presidency. Its center is the Spanish-American War. Messages, proclamations, and executive orders relating to that war fill the volume. A life of the president opens the volume. He was born at Niles, Ohio, on January 29, 1843, of Scotch-Irish stock; his grandfather and father were iron manufacturers.

The sketch follows him from the Poland post office to enlistment as a private in the Twenty-third Ohio Volunteer Infantry in June 1861. The war papers keep the human ledger. Total casualties in the war with Spain are given in the papers. The Army lost 280 killed and 1,577 wounded. The Navy lost 17 killed and 67 wounded. More than fifty thousand troops took the field.
copper-streak-trail:
Copper Streak Trail, by Eugene Manlove Rhodes, is a Western novel of the Arizona desert. Peter Johnson has never been to Silverbell; his own country lies far north, beyond the Gila. Sure of his bearings anyway, he strikes a short cut through the hills, meaning to catch the spur railroad at Redrock and entrain for Tucson.

His horse Midnight does much of the thinking on the page. The horse has held a brisk four-mile walk since three in the morning, thirty-six miles by hot noon, with an hour off at Smith's Wells. He hopes the hill wells run sweet, not alkali, and privately misses the bunch and the soft life of the Forest Reserve pastures. Later talk introduces Boland, a gentleman of few and simple wants who will not work, since that would crowd some worthy person to the wall.
darkwater-voices-from-within-the-veil:
Essays, tales, and poems by W. E. B. Du Bois fill Darkwater: Voices from Within the Veil. Harcourt, Brace and Company of New York first published it in 1920. A postscript says Du Bois writes of self, fathers, neighbours, work, rule, women, children, beauty, death, and war.

He adds one thing only, he says: a point of view from a veiled corner of the world. From it, the drama of men showed itself to him in new light. Prose argument and short verse pieces stand side by side through the book. One passage weighs how little men knew of each other, or of industry, when mass voting came. The book is Du Bois thinking aloud on race, faith, and the future of his people.
doe-osti-17156373-addition-of-b-pond-fra:
D. Petersen of INTERA adds the B Pond area to Hanford's Soil Inventory Model, in document ECF-HANFORD-26-0027 dated September 2026. The model estimates what chemicals and radionuclides sit in Hanford soils, a base input for cleanup decisions. B Pond received liquid waste discharges across decades, and its share must be split among the sites that fed it, a step called fractionation.

Tables give the discharge split from 1945 to 2010 across the 200 East Area pond system. Flow routing equations work out new discharge volumes per site. Appendices then list the updated volumetric inputs, the chemical inventory, and the radionuclide inventory for each B Pond site. A software installation and checkout form closes the package.
doe-osti-2587600-simulation-of-creep-def:
Sagar Bhatt and Mark Messner of Argonne National Laboratory wrote this report, ANL-AMMT-022, on simulating creep in printed metal. Their material is 316H stainless steel made by laser powder bed fusion, a layer-by-layer 3D printing process. Parts in hot service slowly deform under load, and printed parts deform in ways that depend on how they were built.

A physics-based crystal plasticity finite element model drives the study. An orientation-mapping method feeds it, capturing how crystal direction varies through the printed material. The model shows printed microstructures creep faster along the build direction. Texture and grain boundaries strengthen the crosswise directions instead. Add grain-boundary pores, though, and cavity growth makes the crosswise directions creep faster. The model was calibrated for this steel at 725 degrees Celsius, in both as-built and solution-annealed states. Graded microstructures from varied build settings matched experimental creep data well.
doe-osti-2589614-unraveling-fundamental-:
Why silicon nitride crystallizes during chip making, a change that can spoil thin films used across microelectronics, is investigated in Sandia report SAND2025-11589. A large team led by Tesia Janicki, Edwin Chiu, and Aashique Rezwan attacks the question at three scales at once. Lab growth experiments, atom-level simulations, and mid-scale models feed one another.

Chapters measure reaction rates, grow crystalline material on purpose, and test how well the models predict both. One caution stands out: crystal structures borrowed from look-alike materials can mislead simulations, so careful order checks are advised before trusting a run. Future work points toward silicon-rich films. Makers who must keep the film glassy, or crystallize it on cue, get a mechanism map rather than folklore.
doe-osti-2998755-modification-of-fractur:
Rishi Parashar, Dani Or, Yutong Cui and co-workers report on a geothermal project that moved from the Desert Research Institute to the University of Nevada, Reno, in late 2023. Geothermal plants pump water through hot fractured rock and bring the heat back up. If a few wide cracks carry most of the flow, much rock is bypassed and heat recovery suffers. The project aims to plug those easy paths with polymer foam.

The foam starts as heat-sensitive resin droplets carried in the injected water. Once a droplet reaches hot rock, it should foam up, expand and harden in place. First-year work built clear two-dimensional fracture models from glass and aluminium plates to watch flow directly. The team studied foam flow behaviour, curing, and pressure patterns, and wrote the maths for foam travel in simple fractures. Later tests were to check the idea across whole fracture networks.
doe-osti-2999121-evolution-of-the-electr:
Thomas Awe, Edmund Yu, Gabriel Shipley and a large Sandia-led team study a troublesome instability in SAND2025-13115R. In a z pinch, a huge electric current squeezes a metal rod and heats its surface. The electrothermal instability grows from tiny hot spots and engineered surface defects, wrinkling the surface just when fusion designs such as MagLIF need it smooth. An axial magnetic field, along the rod, changes how the wrinkles twist into helices.

The team compared rods with no axial field, a field that ramps with the shot, and a steady field from Helmholtz coils. A new large vacuum chamber with re-entrant viewports was built for the work. Defect tilt alone did not set the final pattern angle. Field direction did: with the field applied at 15 degrees, average pole angles reached about 5 and 10 degrees on the two sides, against about 1 degree with no field tilt.
doe-osti-3004271-tasti-grid-improving-el:
Hillary K. Fishler, Varisara Tansakul, and Thomaz Carvalhaes apply a national analysis platform to one state in Oak Ridge letter report ORNL/LTR-2025/4141. The platform is TASTI-GRID, which helps states target grid resilience spending. This volume covers Tennessee. Its grid faces rapid population growth, rising load, and extreme weather, against a backlog of deferred maintenance.

In 2022 the American Society of Civil Engineers graded Tennessee's critical infrastructure a C, urging the state to clear maintenance backlogs and prepare for growth and storms. The report synthesizes platform data on generation, transmission, outages, and customers for Tennessee decision-makers. A caveat page is explicit: the document is an analytical overview, not a directive, and some source data are incomplete. A stray line in the front matter mentions Mississippi, an apparent template leftover.
doe-osti-3009968-tccsp-site-characteriza:
Site characterization and feasibility report for the Tulare County Carbon Storage Project in California, prepared by Advanced Resources International under DOE contract DE-FE0032264 and dated November 21, 2025. The project would store captured carbon dioxide deep under Tulare County.

Characterization centres on the TCCSP_OBS-1 observation well: mud cuttings, core, wireline logs, formation tests, and fluid samples all feed one geologic model. Sands such as the Moreno and Wheatville show total porosity near 20 to 30 percent. The porosity model matched core measurements closely, though its mineral volumes missed the X-ray diffraction results, a caveat the report keeps visible.
doe-osti-3014502-improving-perovskite-so:
Arizona State University's Nicholas Rolston led this final technical report for award DE-EE0011152, covering May 2024 to October 2025, on perovskite solar module stability. Fielded modules are laser-scribed into cells, and those scribes can seed chemical and mechanical damage. The team asked how the hole-transport layer under the perovskite affects thermal cycling survival.

Three hole-transport layers were compared: nickel oxide, a self-assembled monolayer called MeO-2PACz, and a bilayer of the two. Modules showed surprising thermal cyclability even while generating clear degradation products. Without a fully dense transport layer, traces of moisture and oxygen entering at module edges reacted with perovskite breakdown products and attacked the indium tin oxide beneath. Light-driven cation segregation also depended on inactive areas left uncovered by the top electrode.
doe-osti-3015391-deer-isle-and-stoningto:
Energy reliability for Deer Isle and Stonington, Maine is studied in NLR/TP-7A40-93280, dated January 2026, by Jimenez, Hedalen, and Ingram under the ETIPP program. The island communities sit at the end of the distribution system, so the report builds an outage record first, reviewing Deer Isle's outage data, consumption patterns, and electricity costs.

From that baseline it screens local options against Maine policy, including net energy billing, which lets customers offset bills with output from small renewable generators they own or share through community solar. Program rules from the Maine Public Utilities Commission shape which projects pencil out. The aim is a practical path: fewer and shorter outages for two working waterfront towns without gold-plating the fix.
doe-osti-3018673-the-icarus-light-detect:
Leo Mareso studied the light detection system of the ICARUS T600 detector in FERMILAB-TM-2871-STUDENT. Donatella Torretta and Gian Luca Raselli supervised the 2023 Italian summer student work. ICARUS is the largest liquid argon time projection chamber run on a neutrino beam. It serves as far detector for Fermilab's Short Baseline Neutrino program. The program hunts for a fourth, sterile neutrino. Photomultipliers catch argon scintillation light, localizing each interaction in space and time. The light system drives the trigger and rejects cosmic-ray background.

In August 2023, some photomultiplier signal cables were swapped for a new model. The old cables had shown deteriorating signal quality. Mareso compared laser run data from before and after the swap. The new cables delivered an improvement in signal quality at the electronics. Waveform comparisons across the West cryostat's 180 photomultipliers support that verdict. The analysis gives the collaboration evidence, not anecdote, that the intervention worked.
doe-osti-3027661-research-development-an:
Jalene LaMontagne of the University of Missouri-St Louis reports a Research Development and Partnership Pilot award, SC0023202, running September 2022 to June 2025 and submitted April 6, 2026. The pilot model is personal: take one outside researcher's expertise, here the patterns and outside drivers of tree reproduction, and wire it into the Energy Department's laboratory system. Tree seeding, masting, is missing from most Earth system models.

Activities were connective by design. LaMontagne joined Biological and Environmental Research training and outreach, did directed fact-finding on Earth and Environmental Systems Sciences Division projects. She also met potential collaborators at national labs in Illinois and Missouri to shape joint research ideas. The deliverable is a plan for future work that folds tree reproduction into Earth system change research, plus the partnerships to carry it.
doe-osti-3367088-testing-recommendations: Sandia National Laboratories memorandum SAND2026-21648R, from Josh Yee and Meagan Nelford-Fracassi to Matthew Kury and dated May 5, 2026, recommends how to test components for thermal failure. Peak-temperature pass-fail checks miss slow damage modes like decomposition and creep. The memo proposes tracking a damage accumulation quantity instead. It would be calibrated by linear temperature ramps and rapid ramps to holds: at least five schedules of each style, five repeats apiece, 50 tests total. The document is a short memo of a few pages, and this summary reflects that scope.
doe-osti-3484978-knowledge-graph-for-end:
Pacific Northwest SULI report PNNL-39717, dated August 2026, builds a knowledge graph for tracing an integrated human-Earth system model end to end. Isaias Prieto and Hassan Niazi wrote the report at the Joint Global Change Research Institute. Note the cover prints the first author's name as Preito.

The graph holds edge, fact, and provenance tables, 56 tables in all. Stage tests check row counts table by table. Benchmarks demand exact read-only matches, with changes re-locked and justified. Tests cover input-to-output tracing and one-query assembly. Modelers can prove where every number in a big climate-economy model came from.
doe-osti-3992857-core-model-proposal-376:
Yang Ou, Gokul C. Iyer, Ying Zhang, and James A. Edmonds of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory rebuild the fossil fuel resource curves for GCAM-USA in Core Model Proposal 376, report PNNL-39384, dated July 2026. Resource curves state how much coal, oil, and gas can be won at each cost level, state by state.

The team sorted fuel into grades, from proven reserves to more speculative pools. For crude oil, the new curves cover the full amount already in the global model, so no speculative oil class remains. Offshore oil and gas costs come from the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management through a custom cost function. Coal costs by type come from an ETSAP data set. Sharper curves mean the model's long U.S. energy outlooks rest on firmer ground about what fuel is left and what it costs to get.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BurglassCecil_B: Harold Weisberg, by the evidence of his files, wrote this memo on a meeting with Cecil Burglass concerning the Ray case, the prosecution of James Earl Ray for the King assassination. Weisberg wrote about the King case as well as Kennedy's, and he recorded his meetings with the lawyers and witnesses who crossed his path. The memo is a single page of that working record, kept among his papers in the archive.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FerrieDavidWill:
Southern Research Company, a private investigation firm, prepared a background synopsis on David William Ferrie. The report lays out who Ferrie was on paper. It includes his arrests in Jefferson Parish on morals charges, among them carnal knowledge and contributing to the delinquency of a juvenile.

Ferrie later drew the attention of investigators looking into the Kennedy assassination in New Orleans. A background report of this kind is what investigators build first: addresses, arrests, and reputation in one digest. This one preserves the firm's findings on a man whose name would not stay private for long.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GouldstonPhil_G: Harold Weisberg wrote on March 9, 1973 to a man named Jim, whose surname is illegible, about the commercial representation of assassination books. Representation meant agents and deals: who would sell Weisberg's kind of book to publishers and stores. The surviving record gives the date and subject but no terms, so the letter stands as a dated piece of Weisberg's publishing business.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia: Former Colombian president Álvaro Uribe was known by the nickname El Viejo, the old man. This briefing-book page presents declassified records said to detail suspected paramilitary and drug ties among his circle. The evidence supplied here is the title alone, and the underlying records are not described. Because the claims are allegations in documents rather than court findings, the page is best used as a guide to records that readers must weigh for themselves.
growth-of-the-soil:
Knut Hamsun published Growth of the Soil in Norwegian in 1917, as Markens Grøde; W. W. Worster Englished it here. The first chapter asks who trod the long road over the moors first of all. The answer is a man bearing a sack of food and a few tools. He is a strong, coarse fellow with a red iron beard. That man is Isak, who claims a patch of no-man's-land and builds a farm from nothing.

Isak's wife Inger comes to him, children are born, and the farm Sellanraa grows stone by stone and field by field. Neighbors, a mine, and the modern world press in, yet the book honors the slow work of the soil above all. Hamsun writes in a rich, chanting prose. The novel won him the Nobel Prize's fame and still stands as the great epic of the pioneer farmer.
in-times-of-peril:
G. A. Henty opened In Times of Peril in the spring of 1857, in British cantonments in India. The tale, dated 1881, calls its setting Sandynugghur, bright and pretty before the outbreak. Chapters move through flight, Delhi, and a desperate defense. A tiger saves a party in one chapter, by its title.

Lucknow's besieged Residency and the storming of Delhi fill the middle. Dick urges that two brothers are better than one in a scrape, against their father's wish. Cawnpore and the relief of Lucknow close the campaign. Henty tells the Mutiny as a boys' adventure of empire.
isobel-a-romance-of-the-northern-trail:
James Oliver Curwood's Isobel is a romance of the northern trail, set a thousand miles north of civilisation at Point Fullerton. It opens with Sergeant William MacVeigh of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. He reports his hunt for Scottie Deane, a murderer, across three hundred miles of Hudson Bay shore and sixteen hundred miles of patrol country.

Curwood builds his story from Mounted Police patrols and Barren Lands travel. The harsh beauty of the far north presses hard on his characters, where law, love and survival contend. Isobel herself enters as the woman at the heart of the romance, and the trail romance of the title binds pursuit and passion together. Readers who like adventure stories of the Canadian north, written by one of its most popular early novelists, will find Isobel swift and atmospheric.
jess-of-the-rebel-trail:
H. A. Cody published Jess of the Rebel Trail at Toronto in 1921. He dedicated it to his uncle and namesake Hiram Cody, long since passed within the veil. A hold-up and rebellion open the tale on a river boat, the Eb an' Flo. Captain Samuel and Eben supply the crew's color in the chapter heads.

A newspaper reports the supposed drowning of Henry Randall's only daughter in a middle scene. Her beauty and many friends are described, and her mother is inconsolable. That girl is Jess, hiding on the rebel trail. A forest fire and a ring of death test her before joy at eventide.
nasa-tm-19710069673-photographic-study-o:
E William Conrad, Ned P Hannum, and Harry E Bloomer of the Lewis Research Center filmed boiling inside a rocket engine injector. Their subject was the RL-10 engine during throttled, low power running. At such settings the engine could chug, a rough pulsing combustion fault. High speed motion pictures looked into the liquid oxygen cavity of the injector. A film supplement accompanied the report.

The catalog record explains what the cameras watched. Liquid oxygen boiled inside the cavity while the engine ran in the chugging range. Crew injected helium gas to steady the burning. The films showed conditions as that gas entered. Watching the fault directly helped engineers understand chugging. It also showed whether the helium cure truly worked.
openings-in-the-old-trail:
Bret Harte, the best-known storyteller of the California gold country, gathered nine tales in Openings in the Old Trail. The titles alone sketch his territory: a foothills messenger, Colonel Starbottle pleading a case, and a hotel landlord at the Big Flume. There is also an inheritance in Buckeye Hollow, and a figure called the Goddess of Excelsior.

The opening story plants a boy, Leonidas Boone, under a dwarf fir at burning noon on Casket Ridge. He refuses to move until the tree's shadow creeps to a chosen stone, for no reason he could give. Harte tells the small ordeal with dry humor and close observation. That mixture of local color, sentiment, and irony made his western tales famous on two continents.
pee-wee-harris-on-the-trail: The sample provided here shows only the front matter of Pee-wee Harris on the Trail, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Percy Keese Fitzhugh and illustrator H. S. Barbour, and notes the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. The contents promise a lone figure, three good turns, robbers, a message in the dark, a race with death, and camp scenes, the mixture of the Pee-wee Harris scout stories.
report-of-the-special-committee-on-moral:
New Zealand's Special Committee on Moral Delinquency in Children and Adolescents sent this report to the Prime Minister on September 20, 1954. R. E. Owen, Government Printer at Wellington, printed it that year. The matter had been referred to the committee on July 23, 1954, and its members agreed on the report and its counsel.

O. C. Mazengarb chaired the committee, with R. A. Bloodworth, J. Leggat, G. L. McLeod, Lucy V. O'Brien, J. S. Somerville, and F. N. Stace as members. Four volumes of witness evidence went with the report, plus a large file of written submissions. The report was laid upon the table of the House of Representatives.
sammie-and-susie-littletail: Howard R. Garis wrote Sammie and Susie Littletail, with pictures by Louis Wisa, dated 1910. The contents list thirty-one chapters, opening with Sammie Littletail in a Trap, Sammie Littletail Is Rescued, and What Happened to Susie Littletail. Later chapters cover Papa Littletail's picture, a new burrow, help for Mrs. Wren, and Uncle Wiggily getting shot.
shallow-soil:
Knut Hamsun wrote this novel, here in an approved English version by Carl Christian Hyllested. The translator's preface tells how Hamsun burst on Europe in the autumn of 1888, when chapters of a life-based novel ran in a Danish magazine. Ibsen, Bjornson, and Strindberg then ruled northern letters, yet Hamsun's name was new.

Hyllested traces the long, bitter struggle behind that sudden blaze of fame. Want and defeat had strewn Hamsun's path for years. The novel itself turns to young city lives and thin hopes, drawn by a writer who knew shallow ground by hard personal trial.
sons-of-the-soil:
Honoré de Balzac gives Sons of the Soil to Monsieur P. S. B. Gavault. Katharine Prescott Wormeley turned the book into English. A long dedication opens the volume. Balzac borrows words from Rousseau for its head. I have seen the morals of my time, they run. For his part, Balzac has studied his epoch's march. He publishes this work as a study of it.

His aim is to show a class long passed over. That class is the peasants of France. Writers make criminals poetic, Balzac charges. They all but deify the town working man. None has dared face the country wilds, he says. There a plot runs without cease. Peasant stands against landowner in that plot. The peasant gnaws the soil into a hundred scraps.
the-blazed-trail:
Stewart Edward White dedicated his logging novel to his father, from whose early pioneer life many of Harry Thorpe's experiences were drawn. Contents divide the book into the forest, the landlooker, the blazing of the trail, Thorpe's dream girl, and the following of the trail.

Part one opens with a portrait of the American pioneer as picturesque, resourceful, self-reliant, and bold. Such a man adapts fast, learns from beasts and neighbours, and meets danger with cheerful confidence. He needs little from towns, substituting rawhide for leather and venison for canned goods. White presents woods life as elemental, with epic dramas and a clear eye that marks the advance guard.
the-boy-aviators-in-africa-or-an-aerial-:
Captain Wilbur Lawton wrote The Boy Aviators in Africa, or An Aerial Ivory Trail. Its chapters run from a reunion and stolen ivory to the dark continent and a witch-doctor. The Pool of Death, a traitor in camp, and a battle in the air come next. Slave-traders, gorillas, and a rogue elephant crowd the late chapters.

The first chapter opens in a rush of packs and talk. Harry is told to catch hold, then yelps that a cartridge box fell on his sore corn. A third voice asks if the crew is bound for Africa or on a Coney Island picnic. Billy Barnes, a reporter, is told to be grave now. The talk is brisk and comic, and it sets the crew in motion.
the-cauldron-of-oil:
Wilkie Collins wrote this crime tale, dated 1861 in its heading. The scene is Croix-Daurade, a village about a league from Toulouse in France. Collins notes that the place is known in English military history for a charge of the eighteenth hussars, and in French criminal history for a bold crime.

The story opens in the year 1700 with the cast named one by one. First comes the village priest, Pierre-Celestin Chaubard, a plain, sociable man held in high regard by his flock. Then comes the Siadoux family, headed by Saturnin Siadoux, a widowed oil maker of sixty with five children. Collins presents the case as a plain narrative of a crime found out and punished under strange facts.
the-choise-of-valentines-or-the-merie-ba:
Thomas Nash's bawdy poem, The Choise of Valentines, also called the merie ballad of Nash his dildo, survives only in manuscript copies. John S. Farmer edited it for a private printing for subscribers only, dated 1899 in Roman numerals. The copies used sit in the Inner Temple library, dated about 1680, and in the Bodleian, dated about 1610 to 1620.

Farmer's introduction is candid about the poem's worth. It is doubtful, he says, that the piece was ever printed before, and by merit alone it would not earn print now. Its claim is different: the world cannot afford to lose any document that may bear on knowledge of the past. The edition thus keeps a frank, comic Elizabethan poem in reach of scholars. Line notes, moved to the end of each poem, help readers follow the text without breaking its flow.
the-danger-trail:
James Oliver Curwood's The Danger Trail, dated 1910, lays out seventeen chapters in its contents. They run from The Girl of the Snows and The Mysterious Attack through The House of the Red Death and Jean's Story. A final chapter is named Meleese. Chapter I, The Girl of the Snows, opens on Howland under a polar sky.

For perhaps the first time in his life, Howland feels romance, adventure, and love of the picturesque surge through him. A billion stars glow like yellow, passionless eyes. Behind him the icy Saskatchewan twists white through snow-smothered wilds, with a few lights where Prince Albert, the last outpost of settled life, comes down to the river half a mile away. He looks north into white gloom reaching a thousand miles to the Arctic Sea.
the-daredevil: Maria Thompson Daviess, author of The Melting of Molly and Miss Selina Lue, published The Daredevil in 1916, with a frontispiece painted by E. Sophonisba Hergesheimer and a dedication to Jessie Morson Grahame. Its contents list fifteen chapters with titles such as Sparkling Waves over High Explosives, Vive la France!, That Mr. G. Slade of Detroit, The Impossible Uncle Robert, and Behold, I Am a Spy! Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-emigrant-trail: Geraldine Bonner's The Emigrant Trail, copyrighted in 1910, is present here as title matter and a bare list of parts. The parts are named The Prairie, The River, The Mountains, and The Desert. A fifth part is left unnamed in the list. A frontispiece shows a man bearing a woman back into a dark cavern. No story text appears in these pages.
the-enchanted-april:
Elizabeth von Arnim's The Enchanted April opens in a London women's club on a grey February day. Mrs. Wilkins, down from Hampstead to shop, scans The Times in the smoking room. She stops at a small ad. A furnished medieval Italian castle stands on the Mediterranean. It is to let for April. The ad speaks to those who prize wistaria and sunshine. The thought takes root before she knows it.

Four unlike women share the castle to escape damp lives and dull marriages. Sun, sea, and rest work slow change on each. Von Arnim's tale is light on its feet and warm at heart.
the-first-of-april: An unsigned poem called The First of April, or The Triumphs of Folly is present here only in its front matter. The title page was printed at London in 1777. It gives the work to the author of The Diaboliad. It quotes Shakespeare on the name of fool. It names the price of two shillings and sixpence. A dedication to a famed duchess begins at the end. No verse of the poem itself is included in this portion.
the-great-salt-lake-trail:
Colonel Henry Inman and Colonel William F. Cody wrote The Great Salt Lake Trail. Inman was a late assistant quartermaster in the United States Army. Cody, called Buffalo Bill, was a late chief of scouts. The book's first edition is dated 1898. Its preface surveys the seven historic trails of the plains. All of them cross what is now Kansas. None but the old Santa Fe trail, the preface says, has a more stirring story than the Salt Lake Trail.

Over that highway the Mormons made their lonely Hegira to the valley of the great inland sea. On its shores they founded a city. The preface calls it marvellous in conception, a monument to man's power over hard odds. The same route carried the expeditions of Fremont, Stansbury, and Lander. Over it the Pony Express made its feats of speed.
the-iron-trail: Rex Beach wrote this Alaskan railroad novel. His earlier books include The Spoilers. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. The headings move in his brisk style. The tide takes a hand first. A girl appears out of the night. An Irish prince and a journey to Hope follow. Curtis Gordon shows his teeth, then fails in his cunning. The battle of Gordon's crossing comes midway. A prince becomes a man, then a prince again.
the-ivory-trail:
Talbot Mundy opens this tale in Edward Monty. Its first part is the story of the yerkes. Monty is an elderly English country gentleman. His hobby is fox hunting. His stud runs to four thoroughbreds. The Marquis of Montbar himself keeps him company. Social eminence follows him out hunting. A man of sterling worth is how he is rated. He answers his letters in faultless copperplate.

His horses change at every town and village. He keeps decent company if England offers any. His peers respect him; his park impresses everyone. His secret lies in a hard education. Trials and experience taught him method. The tale will carry that method into Africa. The ivory will test it. Mundy builds an English facade first, then takes it abroad.
the-jubilee-of-the-constitution-delivere:
John Quincy Adams delivered this oration in New York on April 30, 1839. The New York Historical Society heard it. Fifty years had passed since Washington took the presidential oath. Adams opens with a licensed flight of fancy. On the night before that first swearing-in, an angel appears. The angel wears Washington's mother's form. He brings a suit of heavenly armor for the Father of his Country.

Each piece of the armor is named. The helmet is piety, justice, honor, and kindness. The spear is studded with the Declaration's self-evident truths. The sword is the one Washington led armies with. The shield is the Constitution itself. Heavenly hands embossed it with the people's future history. Adams then turns to the thirteen colonies' settlers. English, Dutch, Swedish, German, and French stock mixed in them.
the-last-trail:
Zane Grey published his frontier novel in 1909. Twilight falls over the wild Ohio valley as a traveler nears the end of a rough journey toward Fort Henry. His guide quit that morning with a thin excuse, and his teamster knows nothing of the frontier.

Mr. Sheppard warns the men to speak low so his daughter will not hear their fear. His son Will admits the guide acted like a man expecting trouble or fearing an attack. Grey builds danger from darkness, a lonely trail, and a party that suspects betrayal too late to turn back.
the-lifted-veil:
No author is named on the opening pages of this tale, which begin with a verse motto and a dying narrator. He suffers attacks of angina pectoris, and his physician gives him only months to live. A stranger curse matters more to him than the illness.

He claims foresight of his own death down to its date, September 20, 1850, at ten at night in his study. He can also foresee every event of his last moments, since insight and foresight have wearied his whole life. A tale of second sight, a femme fatale, and dread unfolds from that confession.
the-little-regiment-and-other-episodes-o:
Stephen Crane's The Little Regiment gathers six episodes of the American Civil War: the title story, Three Miraculous Soldiers, A Mystery of Heroism, An Indiana Campaign, A Grey Sleeve, and The Veteran. The title story opens in thick fog, where an infantry column in a roadway looks like a long, low shadow in the mist. Above the ranks hovers a muttering that is one part grumble and three parts joke.

Across a little river, a battered town looms through grey cloud, its belfry still pointing at the sky after bombardment. Guns on distant heights thunder while hidden masses of men and artillery shake the earth. Crane writes war as weather, noise, and confusion, with ordinary soldiers moving through a landscape they can barely see.
the-long-labrador-trail: Dillon Wallace, author of The Lure of the Labrador Wild, wrote The Long Labrador Trail, dated 1917 and dedicated to his wife's memory. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear. The nineteen chapters trace an expedition. Titles include The Voice of the Wilderness, On the Old Indian Trail, We Go Astray, and Seal Lake at Last. Disaster in the Rapids, Caught by the Arctic Ice, and To Whale River and Fort Chimo follow. Closing chapters treat Labrador's Indians and Eskimos.
the-lost-trail:
Edward S. Ellis wrote The Lost Trail, a frontier tale in thirty-three chapters. Chapter one, An Enemy in a Tree, opens on an early-spring afternoon. A sturdy youth of seventeen, Jack Carleton, follows a clearly marked trail through the western part of Kentucky toward the Mississippi River. The contents widen the setting: chapters on the bank of the Mississippi, a visitor from the other shore, the Louisiana shore, a primitive fort, and an aboriginal home.

A recurring figure in the chapter titles is Deerfoot, whose maneuvers get a chapter of their own. Titles like At Bay, The Eavesdropper, Within the Wigwam, and Pursuer and Pursued promise chases and reversals. Ellis writes the kind of frontier adventure in which a boy, a trail, and a skilled Native scout carry the action.
the-patrol-of-the-sun-dance-trail:
Ralph Connor wrote The Patrol of the Sun Dance Trail. The contents list twenty-one chapters, from The Trail-Runner to Why the Doctor Stayed. Chapter One opens high on a hillside among jack pines in Kicking Horse Pass, where the Union Jack marks the headquarters of Superintendent Strong of the North West Mounted Police.

Strong's duty is to keep law and order along the Canadian Pacific Railway construction line. Below, a dark, wiry man comes running up the tote road, panting and streaming with exhaustion. He turns up a side trail toward the flag and struggles to the wooden shack. Connor opens a western tale of police, railway builders, and the peoples of the passes.
the-pupil:
Henry James wrote the novella presented here in the Le Roy Phillips edition published at Boston in 1916, following the Definitive Edition text. A young tutor named Pemberton arrives to discuss taking charge of an eleven-year-old boy in the Moreen household.

The opening chapter stays on an awkward negotiation. Mrs. Moreen talks warmly about feelings while avoiding any mention of pay, and Pemberton hesitates to raise money at all. The boy Morgan is sent out for a fan and returns without it, already showing the sharp, difficult character the tutor will have to handle.
the-rainbow-trail: Zane Grey calls his romance a sequel in spirit, opening with a foreword and chapters set at Red Lake, a sagi, Kayenta, and a hidden valley. Headings follow a trail through hogans, desert trials, a place called Surprise Valley, Navajo episodes, wild justice, and a final approach to Nonnezoshe at the foot of the rainbow. Only the title pages and contents list are present here, so the desert narrative itself does not appear.
the-u-p-trail:
Zane Grey frames his western novel with a long passage from Robert Louis Stevenson praising the railway age. Stevenson calls the line pushed through an unwatered wilderness an epic subject, mixing gold, violence, makeshift towns, and frock-coated gentlemen behind the work. Grey then begins his own story in the early eighteen-sixties.

Chapter one follows the old trail westward from the broad Missouri across Nebraska's grassy plains toward Wyoming. Buffalo herds, wolves, trappers' campfires, rocky gorges, and high passes fill the journey onward into Utah, Nevada, and California. The opening builds the land itself into a character before the human drama of the Union Pacific route unfolds.
the-white-devil:
No author's name is printed in the pages preserved here for the tragedy The White Devil. An address to the reader defends publishing the play at all. The production, the writer complains, was acted in a dull winter time. It played in an open, black theatre, lacking a full and understanding auditory. That audience, he says, is the only grace and setting-out of a tragedy.

Playgoers since resemble ignorant asses at stationers' shops, he adds, asking for new books rather than good ones. Accused of slowness in finishing, he answers with Euripides. The Greek composed three verses in three days, against another writer's three hundred. The other's verses would be read for three days, his own for three ages. He praises Chapman, Jonson, Beaumont, and Fletcher while expecting detraction, ignorance's sworn friend.
tom-slade-on-mystery-trail: Percy Keese Fitzhugh wrote Tom Slade on Mystery Trail, illustrated by R. Emmett Owen and published by Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1921. The Boy Scouts of America approved the book. Fitzhugh also wrote the Roy Blakeley books and other Tom Slade titles. A contents heading begins at the end of what is present, but no chapter titles follow it. The title and copyright pages are what is held in this record, so Fitzhugh's story itself does not appear.
tom-swift-and-his-wizard-camera-or-thril: Thrilling Adventures While Taking Moving Pictures is the subtitle of the Tom Swift wizard camera story by Victor Appleton, presented through twenty-five chapter headings. A strange offer and a man in a snow bank open the book. Later headings travel to India for an elephant stampede and lion fight, then snap an avalanche, a native battle, a jungle fire, and a volcano's molten rim. An earthquake concludes the list. Chapter one is announced without text following. The contents list alone is shown in this record.
un-sc-res-colin-powell-s-february-5-2003:
Colin Powell, the United States secretary of state, addressed the Security Council on February 5, 2003, to make the case for war with Iraq. He spoke for more than an hour, using tapes, satellite photos, and a small vial held up for the cameras. Millions watched the session live.

Powell argued that Iraq hid weapons of mass destruction and mobile labs for germ warfare. He said Baghdad had failed its last chance to disarm. No such weapons were found after the invasion weeks later. The address is now studied as a famous failure of intelligence and persuasion.
un-sc-res-zulfiqar-ali-bhutto-s-farewell:
Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto, Pakistan's foreign minister, gave this farewell speech to the Security Council in December 1971. The Council had just voted on the war between India and Pakistan over East Pakistan, soon to become Bangladesh. Bhutto charged that the Council had failed his country at its hour of need.

He closes by tearing up his papers, declaring he would not be party to a shameful surrender, and walking out of the hall. The scene became one of the most famous in UN history. The speech itself is a fierce attack on great-power politics, in the speaker's own words.
vanguards-of-the-plains-a-romance-of-the: Margaret Hill McCarter, author of The Price of the Prairie, wrote Vanguards of the Plains, a romance of the old Santa Fe Trail, issued by Harper and Brothers in 1917. She dedicated it to the memory of the men who defied the desert, walked the prairies boldly, and died bravely while building a highway for a westward-moving empire. Pages present here hold front matter only: title pages, that dedication, and the start of a contents list whose first part is called Clearing the Trail. The story itself is not shown.
voyage-of-the-paper-canoe-a-geographical: An old Project Gutenberg header identifies this file as Voyage of the Paper Canoe by N. H. Bishop, released as etext number 1082 in October 1997. The pages present here are that header only, with its talk of volunteers, donations, and keeping the file whole for the next readers. No title page, contents, or lines of Bishop's journey down the American rivers in a paper canoe are shown. The header alone names the work, its author, and its place in the Gutenberg list.
vril: Edward Bulwer Lytton wrote Vril: The Power of the Coming Race, dated 1875 in the file header. Pages present here hold that header, the doubled title, and a bare list of chapter numbers running past twenty, so the novel itself is not shown. The list skips from chapter sixteen to chapter eighteen, a gap the pages do not explain. Nothing here names the underground race, their strange power called vril, or the traveler who finds them. Readers learn only the frame of Lytton's tale of a hidden world below the earth.
